speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and . Queen's) :
speechtext:
There is already on the Order
Paper a motion standing in my name, dealing with, the question of the hours of meeting and closing our business on Wednesdays. I regret that the Prime Minister, in this motion, is abandoning at once the Wednesday evening recess. There are strong reasons which can be urged in favour of continuing that recess. I am confident it makes, not only for the comfort and convenience of members, but for the efficient administration of the business of the House. If members know that they will have one evening a week on yrhich they are free to make engagements, they will adapt themselves to that; but if they have no evening free in which they can make engagements, they will take an evening off whenever it suits them, and there will be a lack of attendance. On the Orders of the Day:

Mr. Speaker, I wish
to draw the attention of the Government to an item which appeared on Saturday in the Montreal papers regarding the commercial treaty with France. The item states that the commercial treaty with France, signed on behalf of Canada by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) in the month of January last, will become effective on the 27th of this month. I might say that I have on the Order Paper a motion for the production of that treaty. . When the motion came up on March 4, the Prime Minister asked that the motion stand, and on March 7, the same answer was given. Is it true that the treaty .was signed on behalf of Canada in the month of January, and that it will become effective on the 27th instant? Why is the Government keeping the people at large, the manufacturers who wish to do business with France, and members of Parliament, unaware of the contents of that treaty until it becomes effective?

Mr. Speaker, I will answer the last question first. The Government has not been keeping the contents of the proposed agreement secret to the detriment of manufacturers.

or any other business men of this country; rather the opposite was the point held in view. It is true that an agreement was come to, and that it was signed by myself when I was on the other side in the month of January, and it was signed by the then Minister of Commerce, Mr. Isaac. But it is also true that a little after that a change of Gevernment occurred in France, and consequently the signature by the preceding Minister of Commerce was not effective. The measure had itself to be examined and agreed to by the succeeding ministry, so that there was no treaty that was effective, either in esse or in the future, until it became established that the succeeding Government was of the same mind as the preceding and would carry out the effect of the agreement. That was not ascertained until last week. Now, let me say a word as to why the treaty could not just at this moment be laid before the House. I signed for Canada the proposed agreement. Both copies of it were sent to the French Government through the British Embassy; and when the French Government were in a position to sign-and that would not be until the succeeding Government had approved the agreement-the two copies of the agreement were to be signed in Paris and one copy sent to the Canadian Government. So that really we have not the authoritative treaty or agreement until we receive that signed copy which belongs to us and which is now on the way from France.
Hence, if I had give out the contents of the agreement as made between Mr. Isaac and myself, I might have been misleading the whole people of Canada, because it might never have gone into force. At the present time I have what I believe to be pretty close to an exact transcript of the agreement as it now stands after having been signed by the French minister, and I am going to take the responsibility of laying that before the House at an early date-with the remark that there may be some slight deviations, not very important, in respect to the articles of the agreement as a result of its examination by the minister in France who succeeded Mr. Isaac.
Is it true that the treaty will become effective on the 27th of this month, that is, at the end of this week?
That is the contents of the telegram that I have received from Mr. Roy.
Can it become effective in Canada until it has been approved by this House?
Yes.
A commercial treaty?
Yes.

When did this House
authorize the making of the treaty with France? Are members of this House not to be consulted at all in these matters? I have a distinct recollection of one government in Canada being defeated on that very question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I should like an answer.

May I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if there is any special reason why communication with the French Government should be made through the British Embassy, instead of through the Canadian High Commissioner in Paris?

It has always been the custom that these trade agreements that are made are made through the privity and through the medium of an official of the British Government. I sent the copies which I myself signed through the British Foreign Office. They reached the French Government through that medium, and I expect they will be returned through the same medium.
That was prior to our becoming a nation.
Oh, no. It is said that Canada became a nation a long time ago, during Sir Wilfrid Laurier's time.

On the motion of Right Hon. Sir George Foster for Committee of Supply:

Mr. Speaker, if I am in order I should like to ask the Government one or two questions before the House goes into Committee of Supply. My attention has been called to certain conditions existing on the Intercolonial Railway at Amqui station. May I ask my right hon. friend the Prime Minister whether he received on or about the 10th day of March a communication from Mr. J. E. Beaulieu, Registrar of Amqui, asking why certain changes pertaining to the night and day agents at Amqui station had been made. I understand from a copy of this communication that the day agent

at Amqui station goes on at eight o'clock in the morning and leaves at five in the afternoon, and that the night agent goes on at eight o'clock in the evening and leaves at four in the morning. This leaves the station without an agent between the hours of 5 p.m. and 8 p.m. and between 4 a.m. and 8 a.m. Mr. Beaulieu states that during the time neither agent is on duty trains Nos. 32, 33 and 34 pass through Amqui, and the people are not in a position to get their freight or express on account of there being no agent there at that time. Any merchandise on No. 32, for instance, is carried on through to Campbellton, and does not return until the following day on another train, and vice versa. If the people of Amqui wish to express goods in the opposite direction they have to send their goods out to Mont Joli, to be returned later. I should like to ask my right hon. friend whether he has referred this matter to the proper department, that is, if he has received the communication. A copy of it was sent to me and I wrote to the General Superintendent enclosing him a copy, 'but I have not yet received an answer from him. Whether it is because officials of the road are instructed not to answer communications or not I do not know. It seems rather strange now that when we ask on the floor of the House for certain information we are not able to secure it. May 1 ask my hon. friend whether he has also received a copy of the resolution adopted by the Council at Amqui, complaining of the same thing, and if so, whether he has given the matter his attention? We trust that this matter will be taken into consideration.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I may point out to
the hon. member that if he has any further remarks to make, or suggestions to offer, he had better avail himself of the opportunity now, because he is limited to one speech on this motion. Similarly, the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), in his reply, will be limited to one speech.

Very well, Mr. Speaker. The resolution that was adopted by the Council at Amqui gave a wealth of details, showing that the village has a population of nearly 4,000, and that there are three other parishes east of Amqui itself. All the goods that have been shipped on the trains I have mentioned are loaded at Amqui for shipment. Now, these people certainly want to have the present condition of affairs remedied, and I sincerely trust that my right hon. friend will attend to this matter in the near future.
He may have transmitted it to some other department, but, as I have stated, I have not been able to obtain any answer. I should be glad to see an agent appointed who would be at the station at all times. It seems unreasonable that these trains should pass by that station, which is an important one, without an agent being there. In the communication of which I spoke, of the 28th February, I mentioned the fact that the officials of the Canadian National Railways at Amqui had allowed certain people to pile lumber on the south side of the station in the yard, in the immediate vicinity of which there are quite a number of private residences; and I pointed out that the owners of these houses were obliged to pay the same rate of insurance as is paid by the lumber yards. I submitted this question to the superintendent of the district, but he informed me that he could do nothing. This lumber could just as easily be piled on the northwest side, where there are no buildings nearby; and there are sidings on that side of the yard as well as on the other. I should like to have a satisfactory answer from the Prime Minister, who I trust will give his best consideration to this matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I should be only too glad to reply to the hon. member, especially as he very seldom addresses the House. I cannot do so, however, if what I say now is to be regarded as exhausting my only opportunity for speaking on this motion. The hon. member asks about a communication which he is informed was sent to me, and I rather gathered that he added later on that he had written me himself. Is that correct?
No.

mailed.

not come to me personally unless they were so directed. However, I shall look into the matter and see that proper steps are taken in respect of both.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
ernment giving to Parliament the fullest information with respect to any questions which hon. members care to address to the ministry in regard to the national railroads.
Let me just say this further word: If public opinion is to be formed in an intelligent manner on this important question it can only be so formed by having before the country the fullest available information on which to base opinion, and that information is possible only by the Government supplying it through the medium of Parliament. I think the amendment is so reasonable on its face that it requires no argument for its support.
I would draw the attention of the House to this one feature in conclusion-while the amendment does assert the right of Parliament to full information, as one of the fundamental rights of a body such as this-which is representative of the people at large and with respect to a great property which is owned by the people themselves-it says nothing as to the form in which that information is to be supplied. It is customary in this House to have information given in answer to questions addressed to the ministry, or on motions for the production of papers; and sometimes the information is given through special committees. Nothing is said in this amendment as to the particular form in which the information is to be given; that is for the Government to decide; but it does assert the undoubted right of Parliament to the fullest information in respect to any property that is owned by the people of Canada, the management of which is in the hands of the Government and for which the people, as taxpayers, become liable, especially when, as in the present instance, there are gigantic deficits to meet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have to thank my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) for extending to me the courtesy of notice that this motion would be brought before the House to-day. He did not, however, err on the side of generosity, as the first intimation of it came to me half an hour before the debate at 2.30 this afternoon. I am glad, though, that the motion embodies a subject that is well worthy of the consideration of Parliament, and I shall take the opportunity later to invite, through a fitting channel, expressions of opinion from both sides of the House after the pros and cons are laid 
before hon. members as fully as is possible during the course of this debate.
When the railways of this country were ' assumed as a national property, the question at once confronted the Government as to what system of management would be the best, having regard to the public interest for the operation of those roads. The Government, two or three years ago, found itself in possession of some 17,000 miles of railway, with, all the appurtenances that go with a great railway system in these times, and with the tremendous staff of employees and all the subsidiary activities that circle around anything of the nature of the Canadian Northern or, as it is now, the Canadian National Railways. Until then this country had never faced such a problem. We had for many years operated a railway between the Maritime Provinces and the city of Quebec, and later the city of Montreal-the Intercolonial railway. That railway was constructed and operated not exclusively as a business enterprise. It was constructed in large degree for laudable political purposes, and in its operation through all the years under the Department of Railways and Canals undoubtedly regard was paid to the fact that it was so originally constructed, and there was general consent that it was not being conducted on the hard and fast business lines that would be essential were it treated solely as a business enterprise. But even though there was that reason for the operation of the Intercolonial railway under the Department of Railways and Canals in the manner in which I have described, it cannot be said that the results of that operation were anything like wholly satisfactory to the people of Canada, or that the experience of that operation was such as to warrant the adoption of the same methods were another system to come into our possession. Much less was the experience of that operation such as to permit the Government seriously to contemplate the operation under the direct control of the Department of Railways and Canals-in other words, under direct political control -of a system of the immense magnitude of the Canadian National railways.
I cannot conceive that any Government that had first concern for the well being of such a railway system, or of the country that was the owner of that system, would for a moment think of undertaking the operation of that system-the largest in point of mileage in the world to-day- merely as a departmental activity, as we

operate other services under the Crown. The conclusion then arrived at all hon. members know. It was decided to try the plan of corporate operation; to give this system the same chance to succeed as a business enterprise that other rival or corresponding systems had the world over; and to see what success that system could have under the best conditions that could obtain.
That decision having been arrived at and having been approved by Parliament, the question then presented itself, as to how far it was consistent with the operation of our Canadian National Railways thereunder, that questions concerning only the relations of the operating board to the patrons of the road should be subject to the daily review of Parliament-in a word, to that summons, review, and control of Parliament that undoubtedly Parliament historically has exercised, and must exercise, in relation to services directly under departments of the Government. Well, if it has not been manifest to hon. members not so closely associated with the work as those of us in the Government, it must at least be manifest to those who come closely in contact with operations, that if all matters between the board of directors and the pat-, rons of the road-all things connected with its operation-are to be subject to motion in this House and to disclosure by the production of documents and papers from day to day, the same as any activity of a department of Government, we are right back where we were with the Intercolonial; we are under political control. And we reach a position that to my mind seems to be anomalous, and wholly inconsistent with the corporate management of the road.
While there is corporate management, there remains the answerability and responsibility of the Government for the success of the system. That we cannot dispute. But there is no immediate accountability for the day to day procedure of operation. If there is to be then our officers subject to our direction must operate the road; but our officers subject to our direction are not so operating. The board of directors is independent of Government control and direction; and that being so the Government from day to day cannot be answerable for details of operation, or for what takes place in the ordinary routine of operation between the operating directorate and the patrons of the road.
Now, let us assume that the Government should demand from the directorate, and bring down to Parliament from day to
day, all correspondence that takes place between the directorate and patrons of the system having relation to, say, the price of coal purchased at one point or at another point; or in relation to the situation of a pile of lumber in a little village, or as was instanced already this afternoon, whether that pile is on the northwest or the south side of the track; or in relation to details of purchases; or in relation to details of contracts-let us assume that these are exposed in Parliament, say, and attacked by the Opposition. In that event, is the Government in a position to defend? Those matters did not take place under the direction of any officer subject to our control, they took place under officers subject to the board of directors, for whose general conduct of the system the Government must be answerable, but for the details of whose conduct from day to day those directors are answerable as the directorate of the system. Therefore, there would be no one in a position to defend, there would be no one who could possibly be in possession of information that would enable him to defend.
But even a greater absurdity than that would arise. Owing to the immensity of the system it would be wholly impossible for Parliament to do its work, if it were to attempt from day to day as part of its duties to review the operations of that system, and if the Government were called upon from day to day to account for this or that action of the board of directors in matters of daily operation of the road. Consequently, a position from both those points of view would be taken which could not be sustained-could not be sustained, on the one hand, because the time of Parliament could not be directed to it, could not be absorbed in the effort, and, on the other hand, because it would result in holding the Government responsible from day to day for that which, unless it exercised direct political control from day to day, it could not possibly assume the responsibility.
There is another consideration, too. This system is in daily competition with the greatest railway system in the world, the Canadian Pacific railway, a system with a mileage somewhat less than ours, but which, in the various activities that come under it and in the immensity of its operations, is as yet the greater; a system perhaps the best managed of any very great business enterprise in the world to-day. Now, our system is in competition with that system. In the great body of its activities, it must,

in order to have work to do, in order to get a paying business, perform services in competition with the Canadian Pacific Railway system. I want to put it to this House: how is the Canadian National Railway directorate going to make a success in that fight for business, going to make a success of its efforts to compete with the Canadian Pacific, if every day it is subject to having every action of the board of directors and of its agents and officers disclosed to the public and to its competitor while on the other hand the competitor need disclose nothing at all?
In that connection, the hon. gentleman has said: Unless you are ready, in some form or other, to bring down all the information concerning the operation of the -road-and I am good enough, he says, not to tell you the form in which it should he brought down; I do not know what difference the form makes; if it has to come down it has to come down and this is the only way to get it down-unless you do as you did with the Intercolonial, answer in the House for, and expose to Parliament, every detail of operation, then the system will be generally suspected in the public mind as being merely a great instrument or engine of political patronage. That is the only way, he says, in which you can preserve this road from the suspicion of being a politically controlled organization. Well now, is that the fact? The Canadian Pacific Railway Company would refuse to any man or to any parliament the disclosure of business that is its own; it knows that it cannot conduct the administration of that great enterprise and at the same time disclose to everybody just what it is doing from time to time. Not that what it is doing is wrong, hut every business enterprise knows that it is impossible successfully to conduct a business, impossible to get the advantages which every business must get if it is to succeed, if everybody doing business with that enterprise and the public generally is to know all its moves on all parts of the chess board from morning till night and from day to day. But because the Canadian Pacific does not have to do that, is it shrouded in mystery? Not at all. Why should it be shrouded in mystery any more than any other business? Why should the Canadian National Railway system be shrouded in mystery any more than any other road? Or why should it bq enveloped with the suspicion that because it conducts its affairs in the way any other enterprise must conduct its affairs, it is merely an engine of political patronage? Again is that

the fact? The hon. member reads from a newspaper

a newspaper 4 p'.m. which, I regret to say, though quite within its right, has always opposed the absorption by the Government of these roads, notwithstanding the fact that no thinkable alternative presented itself except the one we adopted; a newspaper which doubtless still takes that attitude. But has the hon. member brought anything forward to support the conclusion arrived at by that newspaper? What is there in the way of evidence that the Canadian National directorate are to-day merely the spokesmen, the instruments of this Government for political purposes? Everything in the way of evidence shows exactly the contrary. The manager of that system is on record time and again, the last time not later than a few weeks ago. as saying that frbm the hour that he took control of that system as manager there has not been an effort or the shadow of an effort to influence him politically one way or the other. Whatever may have beeiU the success of that system under Mr. Hanna and the board of directors that now control, one thing is certain, that nothing in the way of failure can be attributed to influence brought to bear by this Government or by this Parliament. The Government has given them every opportunity to make the road succeed under the business conditions that prevailed. There has been no political control; there has been no patronage of any sort. No one connected with the road, from the bottom to the top; no one on that directorate, would to-day say that there has been any attempt whatever to influence him or to influence the directorate in the control that we said in the first place would be theirs if they took the responsibility of managing the system. Consequently, there is nothing whatever in the contention-I care not from what source it comes, whether from Montreal, from Toronto, or from anywhere else in this Dominion; whether from low or high estates-there is nothing in the contention and nothing whatever in the suspicion, nor does the suspicion generally exist, that there has been anything in the way of political interference with the management of the Canadian National Railways.
I think it will be obvious that if the Can!"'" adian National directorate are to be compelled to answer to resolutions, which by the dozen may be put upon the Order Paper of this House every day, calling for copies of correspondence, for the disclosure of every fact and of every deed con-

(i nected with the operation of the road,
1 they will be put under a disability that their great competitor is not under at all. Should we do that they might well say: You shackle us in the management of the road; you refuse to give us that latitude and freedom of management that every successful business must have; you there-i fore will have to take the responsibility of failure-we do not. That would be the position they would logically assume. I venture to say that no board of directors, no president and general manager who would be big enough for the tremendous task of operating that system to-day, would undertake to assume such responsibility under conditions that would be brought about were this amendment to be adopted.^ I am quite aware that there is to be said from the other standpoint much that is plausible and much that is more or less difficult to answer. I know that it is a fact that the board of directors of the Canadian National railways are dealing virtually with the funds of the people of Canada. I know that Parliament, and Parliament alone, is responsible to the people for the disposition of the moneys raised by taxation; consequently I know that there must be ample facility for the exercise of the control that goes with and is inseparable from responsibility. The difficulty has been to envolve a line up to which you can go in disclosing to Parliament the affairs of the system and beyond which you cannot go if the system is to succeed. Just where that is to be it is very difficult indeed to say. We have brought down certain particulars in relation to the management of the road. Some questions have been answered where it appeared to the Government quite certain that the answering of them or the furnishing of the return to an order of the House could not prejudice the position of the company. I do not think that as yet any very clear principle has been evolved. It is true that the report of the board of directors comes down from year to year, and it is true that that shows what the board of directors of a private system discloses to its shareholders. I do not know that it is impossible to go further than that; I would not like to assert that it is wholly impossible. I know there must be such information at some time as will enable Parliament properly to judge as to the general management of the sytsem and to say whether or not the board of directors that we have put in charge have, in the main,
properly discharged the responsibility placed upon them. That information must be given; but if this resolution passes, it is certain that much that is unfortunate will happen, but very improbable that what is most desirable will actually result. This resolution means simply a return to the old system of political control; it stops nowhere short of that end. Pass this resolution, and you put the system under political control. What is to be done? It has occurred to me that if Parliament set to work, say, through a committee of this House, to study this specific question in order to evolve some rule that could be followed, looking to the discharge of the obligations of Parliament, it would likely result in something definite and concrete. That committee could bring before them those who have to do with the operation of the system, the officers of the road, the president of the road, and if they so desired, touching the subject committed to them they could bring as well officers of the competing road or of other business enterprises of this country. Having done so, they would clearly see just what it would be impossible to do, and I think likely they would be able to evolve something that it would be possible to do, and that would be amply sufficient to put Parliament in possession of all the information that Parliament would require to come to an intelligent decision on those issues that Parliament alone can decide. It is said: "This resolution states that anything of a confidential nature need not be brought down, but that everything that is not confidential must be brought down." What is there that in its nature is confidential?
For example, suppose the Canadian National railways has been engaged, as it is, in the purchase of coal; suppose it buys at one price at one point and at another price at another. Its competitor does that. Now, it takes twenty cents out of every dollar of the earnings of the road to pay for its coal, so coal is a great factor. Its competitor is able to buy just as cheaply as it may at that point or at this. At some points its competitor can get its coal cheaper than at others. If the Canadian National Railways is to Compete on anything like even terms with its competitor, it must be able to do the same.
Is there any duty on coal used on the railways in this country?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: 53 cents a ton. In the West they are using Alberta coal.
Will the Prime Minister say that the price of coal is not public property at every point in Canada where coal is sold? Is the price not known to everybody?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am informed very
definitely that it is not, and I think that will be the conclusion of the committee if one is appointed. Under the old system, though, that was the case; the very fact that the disclosures had to be made to Parliament from day to day resulted in the system having to pay the very same, and that meant the very highest, price at every point all along the system. It is possible, if we pay the price, to do that with the Canadian National Railways. [DOT] Put it under political control, and that is one result that is going to occur. But that does not put it in a position to compete with the Canadian Pacific, or to conduct its enterprise with those attributes of success which are the property of every business enterprise that gets along at all. That is only an illustration; but could it be said that the price of coal or the correspondence relating ot the purchase of coal is a confidential matter? There is nothing confidential about it that does not appertain to virtually every matter connected with the operation of the road. Therefore, the reservation that is embodied in the resolution is no reservation at all; That reservation would not protect the resolution, because it would not protect the system; it would not allow to the system anything at all of the latitude it must have,' unless it is to be so shackled and bound down that a success cannot be made of it. Consequently, it seems to me impossible that the resolution, as drawn, can be accepted. I need not refer to the obvious fact that, moved in amendment to Supply and particularly moved as it was by the leader of the Opposition in terms of criticism of the course which the Government has pursued in this regard, it is a motion of want of confidence as well.
I want to say this as well in relation to it. The senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has on the Order Paper, if I am in order in referring to it, a resolution in which he calls upon the House to establish a Select Standing Committee on Canadian National Railways and Shipping. That resolution has not yet come up for discussion. It has been suggested-and the suggestion appears to me to be one well

worthy of sympathetic consideration, that when the resolution comes up, it might be well for the House to consider whether or not the first duty with which that committee, if it is appointed, should be charged, should be the determination of this very subject that is launched in the resolution now before the House. I think I have said enough to convince hon. members on both sides, especially hon. members who have had to do with business matters, and particularly in connection with great business undertakings, with such closeness as to make them see what is going to result if the resolution passes, that a resolution in such terms cannot receive the favour of Parliament, because the carrying of it out is a reversal of the policy which "this Parliament has adopted; it is a reversion to a policy which, applicable to one very small system, failed, and which, applicable to a system of the immensity of that which we are now responsible for, must result in little less than chaos.

The leader of the Government (Mr. Meighen) has referred to a resolution standing on the Order Paper in the name of the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). That resolution is considerably down on the Order Paper and, in the ordinary course of events, it might not be reached. Might I ask my right hon. friend if he will give an opportunity for the discussion of that resolution so that it may be considered?
