speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the speech of the
Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) is, in one sense, like a lady's letter, the pith of which is generally found in the postscript. I find that my right hon. friend, while arguing for a time in the spirit of what I suppose he thought was sweet reasonableness on the merits of this question, a moment or two before he sat down suddenly cracked the party whip and said: "This is a vote of non-confidence." If my right hon. friend had felt strong on other grounds, he would not have introduced that at the last moment. A motion of this character is only a vote of non-confidence when the Government sees fit to treat it so. It is quite possible, I understand, in our Parliamentary institutions, to present a motion of this kind which will

not be a motion of non-confidence and which should not be treated as such. There are many precedents, if time permitted one to cite them, in which motions made in amendment to Supply are accepted by the Government because they assert some sound proposition which the Government do not wish to oppose. There have been many such cases. In my own experience. as Minister of Finance I have voted for amendments moved to Supply, if my memory is not mistaken, and I think myself that when my right hon. friend insists on making this a party issue he is not acting wisely. I would personally have been very much better pleased if he had said:
" Why, this asserts one of the first principles of free parliamentary government, and I am going to accept it and stand by it." That, I think, would have been the wiser policy, rather than to have told his friends that they must vote against the amendment because it is to be deemed a vote of want of confidence. There is unfortunately a tendency in parliamentary government, perhaps everywhere in these modern times, to move perhaps towards autocracy. It is complained even in England to-day, in the Mother of Parliaments to which we look for guidance and direction, that there is a tendency for the government there to take to itself too much power and make members of parliament, even those supporting the government, feel that after all there is not very much for them to do. If that tendency exists there, certainly it exists in a more marked degree in Canada. It has been a just cause of complaint that hon. gentlemen opposite have again and again resorted to government which ignores parliament. I do not want to go back to the days of the war. They had to do many things then by Order in Council which I approved of, and I am not censuring them for that. But in these days the tendency of this Government from day to day is to undertake to do things and be absolutely indifferent as to what Parliament thinks about it. Why, the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) comes here today and tells us that he has made a treaty with France. He has not told us up to this very moment the exact terms of the treaty, he has not even told us who signed it, except that he signed it himself. Then, a little later, he said that it was customary to do these things through the British Embassy, but we do noe even know whether the British Ambassador signed it. My right hon. friend coolly tells us that he will bring
down a document which he thinks will be something like the treaty, and lay it on the Table, and in the meantime he is going to put the treaty into operation at once. That is the way hon. gentlemen opposite treat Parliament. That has not been the custom in the past, and every hon. gentleman in this House, no matter on what side he sits, should resent such a tendency, and show his disapproval of the growing autocracy of the Government.
We had another case in connection with the luxury taxes. This House spent many days, and properly so, in assisting my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to prepare a system of luxury taxes;-I am not criticising his bringing down those taxes, but I say we spent a great deal of time considering them. He received the help of Parliament; there was no adverse criticism; on all sides he was helped. Then one day in the middle of the Christmas season he coolly steps in, and by Order in Council abolishes the tax. We are always told about Christmas time that we ought to buy early. The shopmen say they hope we will buy early, that we should have regard for the hard-working clerks, and that it is to our own advantage to have a large field to select from. All wise men, I suppose-and that would include members of parliament and their families-observe that principle and buy early. Last Christmas, after they had made their purchases, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance stepped in at the eleventh hour and abolished the tax; so the late comers did not have to pay the tax at all. It is undoubtedly the right of the Governor in Council to reduce taxation, while they have not the power to increase it, but I question the wisdom of a sweeping change of that kind made by Order in Council, even in the direction of reducing taxation.
These are illustrations, I say, of the tendency of this Government to play the part of the autocrat and to ignore Parliament, and never have they ignored Parliament in a way that was more open to criticism than in the case that was presented to-day when with respect to the great railway service of this country, involving an admitted loss last year of $70,000,000, we were told we have no right to ask for information, for that is really what it means. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister said that if we had all these details, Parliament never could attend to them, the time of Parliament would not permit. That would have some force if the right hon. gentleman were right in his assumption that all

these details were going to be brought before Parliament. We have the right to-day to bring all the details of the Department of Public Works, for examples, before Parliament, but nobody does it. There is here and there a case in which information is asked for and brought down but we do not burden Parliament with all the details of the Department of Public Works. It is the same with the Department of the Interior, a large department that spends great sums of money; we have the right to ask for all the details in connection with that department, but we do not do it; we ask only for certain details on matters of prominence, matters which have been questioned by somebody, or matters of particular concern to some section of the country; and we get the information. If we were to carry out with respect to all the departments what the right hon. gentleman implies we are trying to do with regard to the railways, we could not carry on business at all. My right hon. friend raises this ghost of massed details which we could not handle when he knows perfectly well that if we had the right to get all these railway documents we would not demand the full details at all. What is the difference, as a matter of principle, between the details of the Department of Public Works or the Department of the Interior and the details of the railways? I have not seen any explanation of that. If we have the right to ask the Government to lay on the Table a return in regard to an expenditure in the Department of Public Works, or the Department of Militia and Defence, or the Department of the Interior, by what principle can it he wrong if we ask for similar information regarding the railways of Canada? The only difference is this: In the one case they are spending a good deal of money, but in the case of the railways they are spending such tremendous sums that they are getting beyond the comprehension of the people of Canada, and we are practically told by the right hon. gentleman that with regard to this immense railway business we have only one privilege and that is to step up to the captain's office and settle when the Minister of Railways tells us he is $70,000,000 behind. That is the position to which he would reduce Parliament. He will not permit us to get any information, but we can have the glorious privilege of paying at the end of the term. My right hon. friend takes exception to our reserva-

tion. The reservation is made in conformity with the general principle we desire to assert. It should be a simply elementary principle in this House that Parliament has the right to demand and receive the public documents in relation to every dollar of public money expended, no matter how expended. My right hon. friend says that that would be making politics of the railways. I do not see what ground there is for that. I do not want to discuss the principle of public ownership; there are some things we ought to discuss to-day,-and some things we had better lay aside for a later date; there are some things we ought to discuss and some we ought not. We are not called upon today to discuss the general principle of public ownership. We are not called upon to-day to discuss the wisdom of appointing a committee to deal with the railways; that is on the Order Paper and we will reach it in due course. We are only called upon to consider this one question: Is it the right of the representatives of the Canadian people in Parliament assembled to receive an accounting of every dollar of public money that is spent from the treasury? That is the principle; that is all the principle. But "Oh", they say, "this is going to make politics of the railways." Sir, there are different kinds of politics. Politics is not necessarily a mean business; politics is the business of the people, and, using the word in its proper sense, I want to see politics jn connection with every administration of the public affairs of Canada. It is not going to frighten us to say that this will make politics out of the railways. Wherever you have a dollar of public money expended, in connection with that you will have politics, using the word in its proper sense; and any attempt that is made to withdraw that expenditure from what you call politics means to withdraw it from the consideration of Parliament and to deny yourselves the criticism of the public expenditure, which is the first and most essential right of the Parliament of Canada. 1 shall not be afraid of politics of that kind, and if, as my hon. friend apprehends, we shall have it, then I say the more of that sort of politics we have the better it will be for the country. You cannot, Mr. Speaker, take these roads out of politics,- using the word, of course, in its better sense. Politics, I say, when it means the safeguarding of the rights of the people and the proper care of their business, is

desirable, and wherever you have the expenditure of the people's money, you should of necessity have politics in that better sense, which means the right to inquire into matters and to be given information as to how public moneys are expended.
I do not desire to discuss the principle of public ownership to-day. It is not in issue at all. But I am going to make this statement concerning that question, that if public ownership can be maintained only by a policy of secrecy; if it can be carried on only by suppressing from Parliament the information to which the people, through their representatives, are unquestionably entitled; if it can exist only by the practice of dark-lantern methods, then I say unhesitatingly that that is enough to condemn it. Why, says the right hon. gentleman, you cannot make these things public. Nonsense! In nineteen cases out of twenty, what my right hon. friend describes as a mystery is nothing but a dream. He declares that dreadful things would happen with regard to coal if disclosures were made. Well, the Intercolonial bought coal for a great many years, and for a time I had something to do with that matter when acting minister of the department. I know the tendency of the coal people to get good prices, and in that respect, let me say, they do not differ from people in other lines of business. But that is a question which you can always meet. And when there was a combination of the coal companies it was always in the power of the Government to overcome that situation and get coal at a fair price. What prices do we pay to-day? Why, Mr. Speaker, who thinks that we are going to get coal cheaper by hiding in the dark and pretending that we are going to pay less for it than is demanded? And there is no mystery about the rates. The rates, which concern the public, are fixed by the Railway Commission; and the purchase of coal, as well as of various other supplies, presents no more difficulty to the Railway Department than the purchase of supplies does to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. There is not a single argument advanced to support the supression of information on this subject which would not apply quite as well to the suppression of information regarding the Department of the Interior or the Department of Militia and Defence, or of any other department of Government. The principle should be recognized in this instance, as well as in every other, that the people have a right to the fullest possible information on matters so vitally affecting their interests, and if my right hon. friend pretends that you cannot carry on business in that way; if he cannot conduct affairs without recourse to this secrecy; if he is going to build up a system of public ownership based on the suppression of facts and the refusal to inform the people of matters in which they are greatly concerned;-if public ownership is to be carried on in this way, then I say that every man interested in the question should [DOT] stand up to-day and demand that the whole system be brought into the light of day and that things be properly done. Let us confine ourselves to the point under consideration. We are not considering the principle of public owernership or the appointing of a committee, or the probao-ility of any vote of want of confidence; let us ignore all these herrings drawn across the trail and recognize the one fact that in this motion we are dealing with the right of the Parliament of Canada to be fully informed regarding the expenditure of the people's money. That is the question upon which this House is asked to vote.

If
we were considering this question in the light of an ordinary department of Government, then frankly, at once, I should have no hesitation whatever in supporting the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition. But it does seem to me that this question is not at the present time in the category of an ordinary department of Government. It is a time-honoured principle, universally recognized in British Parliaments, that in the matter of departmental expenditures the people have the right to the fullest and most complete information regarding the details of expenditures. But when that principle was first adopted, or put into practice, it was under conditions where the whole expenditure was outgoing and there was no corresponding income. Now we are faced with a different situation. I quite agree with my hon. friends that this is not a proper time to discuss the principle of public ownership. In view of the statement presented by the Minister of Railways the other day, what this House has under consideration now is the question, how we can best handle a difficult, perplexing and very discouraging situation. Now, there is a great deal of force, I think, in the argument advanced by my right hon. friend who leads the Government (Mr. Meighen). If we take the stand that every detail of expenditure in connection with our na-

tional railways shall be placed before the HcJuse at the wish of any hon. member, in what position do we place the management of our national system of railways in competition with, for instance, the Canadian Pacific Railway? It is an elementary principle of business that a good business man, one who conducts his affairs successfully, never discloses the full and intimate details of his business to his competitors; and it does seem to me that that is the position in which we should be placing ourselves if we adopted the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition. At all events, the Government, as I interpret the amendment, would be committed to bring down any information that was asked for, saving such information as might be of a purely confidential character. Now, information of a purely confidential character in connection with the administration of our railways would probably be confined to a very narrow field. At the same time, however, I recognize that the people have to foot the bills in connection with the deficits on these roads, and that does place upon Parliament, in connection with the administration of the national railways, a responsibility which we cannot evade. The whole question is one filled with difficulty at the present time. In my judgment it is one that should be approached in a spirit free from any taint of partisanship, and for that reason I am quite in accord with the suggestion, as I understood it, that came from the Prime Minister that a special committee selected from the House, should take into its consideration the whole scheme of operations of the railways, and all matters that might be submitted to the House in the interests of efficiency and success in the management of the roads. We have on the Order Paper, as my hon. friend has pointed out, a resolution to be moved by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). Now, it does seem to me that the spirit of that resolution is the best approach to the consideration of the question at the present time. If we are going to discuss in a partisan way across the floor of the House the success or failure in the management of these railways, attributing blame here, finding fault there, defending in one place and explaining in another, how much progress shall we make towards a satisfactory and sensible solution of the question? I, for one, Mr. Speaker, am profoundly anxious to see the consideration of this difficult problem removed, if possible, to the atmosphere of the committee room. I have observed in my experience in this House that when 
hon. members consider questions in committee, we can get a clearer and fairer consideration, a more intimate discussion, and a more unprejudiced exploration into the facts of a case, than we can possibly obtain in the House, where it is natural for us to divide according, shall I say, to our party views upon any matter. And this being a perplexing question, a question fraught with great difficulty and involving immense consequences to the country, I for one should like to see us approach the consideration of it at the present time without any partisanship.
Now I am quite free to say that I am in hearty accord with my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) when he states that this should not be regarded as a motion of want of confidence in the Government. Let me say at once that if I considered it purely a motion of want of confidence, I could not vote confidence in the Government. But I do not consider it as such. I am endeavouring to approach this question from the point of view of what will afford, or offer, the most satisfactory solution of it. In what way can we approach the question and discuss and consider it, free from partizanship, that will afford the greatest possibility of finding a satisfactory solution for the difficulties we are in in connection with it? For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I shall feel bound to vote against the amendment of the leader of the Opposition.

The hon. gentleman has intimated to the House that he is favourable to the resolution standing in the name of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) which is that these matters might be referred to a select committee. Is it my hon. friend's understanding in that connection that such a committee shall have the right to ask any question with respect to these railways that may be thought in the public interest and have it answered?

If I am in order in
answering the question, Mr. Speaker, I would say that I certainly think so. In that connection I may add that such a committee could bring the president or the management of the road before them, and secure intimate and direct information in a way that cannot be secured when a motion is made asking that an ordinary return be brought down to the House. In that way you can explore the whole situation, you can get full information, you can have the opportunity of estimating the efficiency and the ability of the management of these

roads iri a way that is not at all possible by moving for the production of correspondence regarding the purchase of coal, the selection of a station site, the purchase of lumber, or anything else. It certainly does seem to me that this is the sensible inanner in which to approach this proposition.
Mr. FRANK S. CAHILL (Pontiac): I would advise the Prime Minister to peruse the report in regard to the railway situation presented the other day by the Minister of Railways. The Prime Minister this afternoon talked of success as though the government railway undertakings were a success. As a matter of fact, the people are called upon to pay the sum of $70,000,000 for a failure not for a success. The right hon. gentleman also advanced the argument against the amendment that information with respect to the national railways could not be brought before Parliament in the regular way. Now, I understand that the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental railways are subject to audit by the Auditor General's department. I would ask the Minister of Railways if that is not correct?

They are subject to
audit by the Auditor General's department, but I may say for the information of the House that the intercolonial and the Transcontinental railways are being managed by the Board of the Canadian National Railways.

That is my understanding. So it is a fact that all expenditures on the Government railways, outside of the Canadian Northern, are subject to audit by the Auditor General's department. I would like to draw the attention of the leader of the Agrarian party to this fact. I learn by the report presented by the minister on March 17 that operating deficits on the Canadian Government railways increased thirty-eight per cent, and operating deficits on the Canadian Northern increased 151 per cent. Now the Government railways still subject to the audit of the Auditor General's department consist of about one-third of the total mileage of what my hon. friend wishes to call the Canadian National railways. That one-third of the total system makes a better showing because its accounts are submitted to the Auditor General's department. My hon. friend, I think, does not get the point.
Oh, yes, I get it.

One-third of the system at the present time, that is the Intercolonial
and the National Transcontinental Railways, are subject to the audit of the Auditor General's Department, and the deficit on that one-third increased, according to the minister's statement, by 38 per cent, while the deficit on the remainder of the government system, under the dark-lantern method as conducted in Toronto, increased by 151 per cent. That would naturally indicate that there must be some information that should be brought to the attention of Parliament. If one-third of the system, operated under the old method, shows better results than the railways operated under the new method, it would be natural for members to inquire into the cause. For that reason we should have questions in reference to the government railways answered in Parliament. The Prime Minister in discussing the old method of management on the Intercolonial deplored the conditions under that method.
I have the report of the Department of Railways for the year ending March 31st, 1920, and it shows-
What page are you quoting from?

Page 103. My hon. friend will find by a reference to that part of the report that the operating deficits in the year 1912 amounted to, in round figures, $40,000; in 1913, to $47,000; in 1914, to $160,000; in 1915, to $330,000; in 1916, to $450,000. Then the new method of management was introduced and in the following year the operating deficit was $1,200,000. The following year it was $6,000,000; in 1919, $5,800,000; and in 1920, $6,800,000. So I do not see that the old method of operation was so very bad, so far as results go, compared with the present method; the expenditures now are three, four and five times greater than they were under the old method. It is just possible that a part of this deficit is due to bad management without control. It is just possible that if the management were responsible to Parliament a better system would be followed, and that they would be more careful in their expenditures.
As to secrets in connection with the operation of the Canadian National Railways I do not believe there is one thing that goes on in connection with that operation from one end of Canada to the other that the Canadian Pacific are not familiar with twenty-four hours after it goes into effect. Let us consider the operation of trains on the Grand Trunk Pacific between Winnipeg and Saskatoon. They have a

train leaving Winnipeg at six o'clock in the evening, and another one leaving at nine o'clock, three hours later, and both trains arrive at Saskatoon within an hour of each other. How are the management fooling the Canadian Pacific in that regard? Why, the Canadian Pacific know what bad business it is to have two first-class trains arriving at Saskatoon one almost on top of the other. The management of the Government Railways are not fooling any person by that class of methods. Neither do they fool any person in the matter of the purchase of their ties. The Canadian Pacific go into the market to buy their ties, so do the Canadian Northern and the same with the rest of the national railways. There is nothing to be gained, but very much to be lost by this method of secrecy. Yesterday I thought when the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) came in with the fore-runner of	his	resignationthat he would not haye been here to-day to continue	this	discussion.
The hon. minister said to us that he had no solution, and that he would like the cooperation of Parliament. The Government through the minister, is responsible for the administration of the affairs of the Canadian National Railways. They come to Parliament year after year asking on an average for over $100,000,000 annually to sink in this undertaking. The minister says that he has no hope of any better prospects for this railway system. Under those circumstances the logical thing would be for the minister to hand in his resignation, and for the Prime Minister to accept it. But under existing conditions the leader of the Government could not replace him, for there is no constituency that he dare open; therefore the minister is left to muddle along in the same old way. He has no solution, the Government has no solution. There is only one solution, and that is the resignation of the Government. If they acknowledge their inability to deal with matters coming before them, they should resign; and if the succeeding administration are not able to cope with the problems of government they in turn should resign, until finally we do get men who are able to administer the affairs of the country in a businesslike way. Otherwise government is a farce; it does not mean anything. The members of this administration acknowledge that they cannot handle the questions coming before them for solution, yet they hang on to office for dear life.
My hon. friend in his wonderful statement the other day gave some more or less 
inaccurate details. At page of 1052 of Hansard he stated:
In a word, out of every dollar earned we had to pay 75 cents for operating wages, and 20 cents for fuel, leaving 5 cents for all other requirements which totalled 29 cents.
The minister was referring to 1920. I am quite satisfied that his statement is accurate, because he took good care to read it, and I am sure he had some assistance in the preparation of it. Now, if he will turn to the report of the department of Railways and Canals for the year ended March 31, 1920, he will find this sentence on page 19:
It is of interest to note that for every dollar earned in the last year the railway had to pay out over 75 cents in wages.
That was in 1919. Now, the minister comes down here and tells us that in 1920 he had to pay 75 cents in wages, and he proceeded to show by implication that the increase in wages is at the root of all the trouble. He stated:
Rate increases have been given from time to time in an effort to meet increased cost of operation under the McAdoo and United States Labour Board awards, under which the average wage per employee of the Canadian National system in now $1,850 as compared with $709 before the war. The result is the operating pay roll last year was $83,505,072 as compared with $40,606,170 in 1917.
That would lead the public to believe that there had been an enormous increase in wages. Well, if my hon. friend will turn back to page 11, of his annual report for 1919, he will find, under the heading of Whge Increases that the total wages paid in 1919 were $73,000,000. So that the total wage increase, acording to his own statement, is only $10,000,000. And on top of that is given a table of the number of employees on the road, showing that they have been increased by 3442. According to his own statement the average wages would amount to more than $6,000,000, so that the employees of 1920 apparently are only getting about $4,000,000 more than they did in 1919, which is not a very great difference. But his operating deficit has increased $12,000,000; his earnings have increased $13,000,000, leaving a difference of $25,000,000 in that item. There is only from $4,000,000 to $10,000,000 taken up in wages, and yet my hon. friend would attempt to lead the country to believe that the whole difficulty is caused by excessive wages.
Now, we have asked from time to time for particulars, and we have also asked to be informed of the policy of the Government. This afternoon the Prime Minister

said that the Government was responsible for the management. I agree with him. There is no question about that; the Government must be responsible. But his general manager on the question of rates said just a few weeks ago, as reported in the Pembroke Observer of February 3:
I made this statement, that if you would give vs in Canada the same rate as South Australia (1 am speaking of the whole National system) i will pay 5J per cent on the Government debt of 2i billion dollars and 51 per cent on another Billion dollars, and then I shall have 100 million dollars to spare to play with.
Who said that?
Mr. Hanna, the general manager. He advocates an increase of three times the rate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not rise for the express purpose of interrupting the hon. member who is now speaking, but to draw the attention of the House to the fact that when an amendment has been made to a motion that Mr. Speaker do leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Supply, the discussion must be strictly relevant to the amendment until it has been voted upon or otherwise disposed of. The amendment presented by the hon. leader of the Opposition declares, that it is the undoubted right of Parliament to demand and receive copies of all reports, correspondence and papers in relation to the management of every department of the public service, including the affairs of the Canadian National railways. In my opinion this amendment does- not open the door sufficiently wide to enable hon. members to discuss in detail the administration of the Canadian National railways.

Mr. Speaker, I was just going to point out that there must have been some correspondence between the minister and his general manager on this subject of rates, although there is this apparent conflict between them. It is all in line with our argument asking for information. The general manager makes one statement, the minister makes another. We want to have particulars of the correspondence between them. In his statement the other day the minister said:
It Is impossible for British Columbia to grow and ship fruit and lumber at the present high rates of freight. The Prairie Provinces must live from the products of the soil. They cannot p; oduce wheat and other products of their farms and ship it to foreign markets if these high freight rates are to continue indefinitely.
The minister apparently is in favour of decreased rates; his manager apparently is in favour of increasing them threefold.
I merely point this out to show the necessity for giving members of this House some information on which to base a fair judgment on the operation of this railway system. It is impossible to arrive at any conclusions if the ministry insist that they cannot give us information from day to day. I do not think there has been any question put on the Order Paper asking for information that could be considered as strictly confidential, but the minister has replied day after day with his usual stereotyped form that in regard to this service it is not in the public interest to furnish the information desired. I -think the Government would be well advised, at this time, when the people are looking to them for a solution of this railway problem, to take the House into their confidence in every detail of the operation of our national railways and to give us the fullest information possible.

Mr. Speaker, in saying a very few words upon the resolution before the House I should desire very much to avoid what- I am bound to call the unwonted heat of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). That unwonted heat seemed to me to go so far as to blur my hon. friend's memory. He declaimed against the dragging of red herrings into the discussion, and he himself did a good deal in the way of dragging red herrings in-amongst others, the luxury taxes, which had no immediate connection with an amendment regarding railways on going into Committee of Supply. His memory in regard to the luxury taxes, I am quite sure, is not the same as that of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), when he says that no adverse criticism was offered to the luxury taxes at the time of their introduction. My recollection is that a good many hon. gentlemen sitting very close to the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's passed a good many criticisms upon those taxes. I was under the impression that I had criticised them somewhat myself. Now, I object to the proposition that is put forward 'by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's that every view not consonant with his on either the railway question or any other question is a "red herring." We must all have the right to express ourselves honestly and sincerely on various public questions that arise.
On first sight there seems to be a good deal in the contention of my hon. friend who leads the official Opposition that the

Government have brought this motion on themselves because through their Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) the other day they appealed to every member of the House for assistance in the solution of the railway question. It would appear to be a little difficult to give full assistance 5 p.m. without full information, but that is only at first sight. A great many general considerations [DOT] in regard to the management of railroads can surely be discussed in this House that the accounts in regard to the railroad have no bearing upon whatsoever. Apart from that, however, I do not know that my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition offered any argument, except perhaps the old argument that Parliament ought to have full control of the money affairs of the departments of the Government. There is the crux of the whole question. These railroads, for better or for worse, were taken out of the hands of a government department and put under corporate management. I think that the motion of the leader of the Opposition is, to say the least, premature, having regard to the fact that, in the first place, we are going to have at a very early day a general discussion, I understand, upon railroad matters following the statement of the Minister of Railways; and, in the second place, that the tendency of the resolution before the House this afternoon is to prejudge the whole question of Government ownership and damage the experiment of this country in that direction.
I should have thought that before bringing up what I have ventured to call this premature resolution the mover of it would have had some information to give the House as to what is done in regard to roads managed by the government in other nations of the Empire and in other nations of the world. No information of that kind has been given either by the hon. leader of the Opposition, or by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's. All that was contained in either speech was a general statement of principle with which everyone in this House agrees-the principle that government departments in their expenditure should be supervised by Parliament. Now, I am not in a position to give the information about what is done in other countries where government ownership has been adopted, but I am trying to put the case that this motion is premature and meant to damage government ownership, and I judge that that view is supported strongly by the source from which the motion comes.

I think my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) gave a view to the House that was very strong and very much calculated to impress people who are impartial upon this subject. It had an evident effect upon my hon. leader (Mr. Crerar). If all the information usually kept by a business company from a competing company is to be given by the officials of the government road to the officials of a private road which is in competition with it, is it not obvious that the government road is at once put in a position of disadvantage as compared with the competing road? I think that there is no getting away from that proposition. But the ground I want to take is simply this:	that Government ownership was
undertaken under financial conditions with regard to these roads that bristled with difficulty and that certainly were not the creation of any one party in the state and certainly not specially the creation of the party at present sitting opposite to me in this House. I want to impress this further consideration: that confronted with these difficulties the nation, through its Parliament, has made a new departure on a colossal scale, and if that departure is to be successful it must have a reasonable chance, it must have common justice meted out to it. Therefore I consider that the resolution before the House is premature and not supported by the information which we should have had before it was brought up at all.
I distrust any attitude on this great question which is obviously born in an atmosphere of suspicion. I prefer very much to approach this question in the spirit of the helpfulness and co-operation which are absolutely necessary not only among the various political parties in this country, but among the people of this country, if we are to make this great railway system the success which we have faith enough in Canada to believe it can be made.
Now, I would not like to use stronger language than I can justify, but what is the meaning of the talk about "dark lanterns" in this connection? One would suppose that every horn member who does not jump up in a state of great heat and support a resolution brought at very short notice before this House has burglarious intentions upon the assets and the good things of this country. That is the only attitude of mind which can dictate the use of such language as "dark lanterns". Personally I resent that suspicion as far as it pertains to myself. I have had no experience in burglary and I am not carry-

ing a dark lantern. I am approaching what is the greatest public question of the day, I repeat, in a spirit of helpfulness and co-operation, and that spirit I shall maintain until I see better reasons to discard it than I have seen in anything that has been advanced this afternoon.
I do not think the question of parliamentary control of the public purse is, ' strictly speaking, germane to this discussion, or that it should weigh with any hon. member in giving his vote. This is a new departure. I do not say that, if Parliament is still sitting next year, I should not vote in a different way from what I do now upon this question. It may be that the committee that is to be appointed will disclose matters that will change our views. The hon. member for Chatqauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) laughs at the idea that I might vote differently next year from the way I do now on a public question. That only shows his hide-bound partisanship and my openness of mind. They say that the man who never changes his mind has no mind to change, but I would not apply that for a moment to my hon. friend. I do not see that the principle of parliamentary control arises. We are facing a new departure. The Government, as far as I can see, have been open and above-board in their appeals upon this question. I have a firm conviction that the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), who is a young man and who has a political future before him, is engaged in an honest, straightforward and sincere attempt to give this great question fair play, to give a fair trial to the principle of government ownership in regard to our railroads which had got into an intolerable mess and a condition of bankruptcy. As long as that is the spirit which animates my right hon. friend and his Government, he can rely upon my support.

Mr. Speaker, I can understand the difficulty of men who have seen an attempted cross between responsible government and co-operative management, and who have been in doubt which of the parents this hybrid creature most resembles. But I am not going to pursue that line of thought; I will simply say that it explains, perhaps, much of the confusion of mind in which many numbers of the House may rest.
I want to deal with just one side of the question. I am quite sure that the great solution of our trouble is in economy; that the people of the country have not yet recognized the necessity for that economy.
That can be effected only by a reduction of many train services from daily to triweekly or twice-a-week services. As regards taking trains off, the other day I went down to the commission and asked them for certain figures. I found that the train which runs from Moncton to Campbellton was earning about 52h cents a mile one way and about 65 cents a mile the other way, whereas it costs ?2.50 a mile to run a passenger train in this country. That train had been on for years running over a route on which two other trains ran. Are you going to ask this House to decide whether-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must direct the hon. gentleman's attention to the circumstance that the motion before the House, the amendment, has to do with the production of documents, and the question of the operation of the railways, as such, is really apart from the main question. There is, perhaps, no objection to a reference to the railways, but a discussion of the railway problem in general is certainly not the main subject.	[DOT]

I think, Sir, had you allowed me to finish, you would have seen the pertinence of the illustration, because that is all that I am making. That train has been on, as I said, for years. Are you going to submit to this House every decision of the management with regard to the taking off of a train or the making of economies? It is those particulars that the House would attempt to review rather than those which the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) presented this afternoon as to the purchase of coal or supplies, and the railway's dealings with individual customers. The House will take up cases where a train runs through, perhaps, three or four constituencies, and where the constituents are up in arms against what the management considers must be done for economy. Those constituents bring the case to Parliament, and it is a case of "You scratch my back and I'll scratch yours," to use a very vulgar expression. One member says, "I am going, to have-this very same trouble; support me, and I will support you." In other words, this is not the forum in which to consider such questions as that. Consequently, I say: Let us try out the question of co-operative management and see whether that will get results. I am very much in the position of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark). If that method does not succeed, I am prepared to change my mind



about it, but I do not see any prospect of success at present by going out on the lines which we followed in connection with the Intercolonial and getting a repetition of the very evil results we got there.

Mr. Speaker, I very much regret that the official leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has not couched his amendment on sufficiently broad grounds, so the whole question of the administration of the public railways of this country could now be discussed. I realize clearly that the whole House is seized of the fact that the resolution has been placed before us more in a partizan than in a public spirit, and for that reason, I do not see that any member on this side of the House will have any difficulty in voting it down. It is extremely unfortunate, at this stage in the discussion of the railway question of this country, that we should start playing politics with it,-because it is a great issue, and we are going to destroy this country entirely unless the wisest heads in this House on all sides get together and discuss this question soberly and honestly, as the leader of the Agrarian group (Mr. Crerar) has done to-day-give our best judgment and arrive at some conclusion. Because I must confess that, so far, I see nothing ahead but failure. I am one of the members of this House who were strongly in favour of bringing about the nationalization of our railways. I am in no sense a believer of communistic theories or of socialism. I believe, however, in Ruskin-ism. John Ruskin was the first to advance the theory of government control of public utilities. He went no further, and that far I am prepared to go. It is quite evident that it is not enough that we people who put up a few cheques for income tax can look around and say: "Well, we have contributed one-half, or one-fourth of the railway .deficit." With all our trouble to contribute to the income tax, we contribute only about 50 per cent of the losses on the national railways. Something must be done. It is a matter of regret that this resolution was not broader so that we could discuss the whole question. The only thing thiat we can discuss in reality is the question of the production of papers. That resolution brings us back to the old control that we had before we took over the Canadian Northern, the Mackenzie and Mann road. I am not one of those who believe that the Intercolonial was badly managed under government control; the Intercolonial railway was well managed under government control. I .
have travelled upon it many a time, and I know that its trains were just as good as those on any road in America; even the New York Central or the Illinois Central did not have better trains or better service; they were not better managed. The road was in as good or in better condition than any other road at that time in the United States or Canada. As a matter of fact for many years until recently the railway has shown a profit on its operating expenses.
Now what are we going to do on this question? Are we going to sit back and twirl our thumbs and say there is nothing than can be done, and go back to the old idea of management and have all the old troubles? Or are we like sensible men going , to discuss the que'stion here dispassionately without regard to politics? This is a time I say when there is a great industrial war on, and we should all get together the same as we did when any other war was on. Unless we on both sides of the House divest ourselves of our partisan minds on this question, the people of this country are going to sweep out of this Parliament every man who plays politics on this grave issue; for the people look with horror upon these terrible deficits that the railroads are showing. I confess that under this resolution I cannot enter into any discussion as to what causes these deficits, the only thing I can say is that certain documents should or should not he brought down. The question of whether we should have a committee or not will be discussed under another resolution. The idea to my mind is a splendid one but I cannot give any reasons in favour of itt Under this narrow resolution that has been brought in to-day which is an extremely partisan one and was intended for partisan purposes. I expected that we were to have a broad resolution and a continuous debate over some days on this railway question when we could openly discuss everything in connection with the roads. This is no time to talk about autocracy. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) says that we have autocracy in this Government. As a matter of fact while there may be a little bit too much autocracy in government, yet the members of this House have shown a self-denying spirit in the matter of railways, for we put this railway question entirely out of our hands. We have placed it in the hands of an independent body with a view to eliminating entirely parliamentary partisanship and patronage from the management. I say that was self-denial, the entire opposite

of autocracy so far as we are concerned. Whether the question was approached by us in the proper way or not I cannot say. I do not quite agree-I did not at the time- with the method by which the Government put the railways in the control of this directorate. I pointed out at that time that it was a very great mistake for the Government of this country to sign a blank cheque to any Board of Directors in charge of any large work of that kind. I said it would prove fatal to government control of these roads if there was no supervision and that it was wrong in principle. At the same time I , did hot push the matter further, but the results have demonstrated that there is no control whatever over the management of this road. The directors who have been appointed do not control the management; they do not know what is going on there at all. It is entirely wrong to put a business man in charge of a railway enterprise. Of course, I know there are a lot of business men and professional men running all over the country who can tell you more about railways - in five minutes than could' Lord Shaughnessy, for instance; they know it all. I say this is a question for specialists in railroad operation. To my mind, the people who should have been put in charge of the road should have been the best expert operators in their particular line that could be found in America. We should have had on the Board the best specialist in freight traffic, the best specialist in passenger work, the best specialist in engineering, and so forth. If we did that, we should have exactly the same condition that prevails on the Pennsylvania road, and on the New York Central in New York state, two great systems that will compare with the Canadian system. These roads, instead of putting business men on their directorates and making them vice-presidents, appoint the men who know how to operate a road, and make them responsible to the shareholders. The idea of the guinea pig director so far as the management of large enterprises is concerned, this idea of putting rich men on the directorate, is entirely wrong and antiquated.
As I said, the question before us is whether or not we are going to revert to the old system. I agree with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark); I have not made up my mind on any of these matters. I want to see the whole question discussed; I want to have the facts and the figures. It may be correct for us to vote for this resolution, but if we have all the facts be-
76i
fore us, we may find out that it would be wrong to do so. For that reason, I intend to vote against the resolution, and I do not think there is anybody on this side of the House within sound of my voice but would agree that it would be dangerous for us to" take any decided stand on this question until we have all the facts before us. The question is such a serious one that we must approach it with an entirely open mind, and give it our very best consideration. The best business minds in the House, the best legal talent, the .best thinkers must give this matter their personal consideration, and we must approach the question without any party spirit at all. Otherwise, we are liable to lead this country into bankruptcy, and we are mighty close to it now.
As to what happens at a little railway station, well, I have had information handed to me about these railways that would shock hon. members. I have heard rumours of hundred-dollar doors being put on woodsheds anjl that sort of thing. I cannot say whether those rumours are true or not. I do not know whether our roads pay more for coal than they should or whether they take on three hundred men immediately after the Canadian Pacific dismissed them. But rumours of that kind are floating around, and I feel satisfied that the proper thing for this House to do-and the Prime Minister has hinted that he is going to do it -is to appoint a committee to go into this whole question and discuss it dispassionately without politics entering into it at all. Let a committee composed of the three groups in this House discuss the whole question, with power to call for witnesses and papers, and take evidence under oath; I am sure that a committee of that sort that went into the whole question thoroughly would reach a conclusion very easily. I have never seen a committee of the House fail to come to a wise conclusion, if left alone, on any great public question. Take the question of the soldiers' pensions. No country in the world has found a better solution of the pension question than has Canada, and it was largely due to the fact that there was a wide-open committee of members of both sides of the House which went into the whole question.
There is no doubt that there is a tremendous war on between the Government railway and the railway controlled by the Canadian Pacific shareholders and directors. It is a matter for very much regret, because if that war continues, it is going to pull both roads into the hole, and I think

the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific are reaching that conclusion when we see the great fall there has been in the securities of that road. This is a condition that should not exist, because Canadian Pacific shares are one of our premier securities, and it should never be thought by the people of this country that we as a people or as members of Parliament have any idea of destroying the interest or undertaking of that large corporation. If any such a thing should occur it would be destructive to all our securities in this country. There is no doubt that there is a certain amount of jealousy and fighting between the officials of the two systems, and something should be done to stop it. I am satisfied, however, that the lesson has been learned by both managements, and that after we have had this matter thoroughly discussed by a committee of this House and the question has been fought out here, some sensible conclusion will be arrived at. This is a time when we should be more patriotic and desirous of helping our country than of keeping up the political war mind. The question is too serious. The deficits of these railways alone are as great, almost, as the total expenditure of the Government when I came into this House; and when I think of that fact I am shocked and appalled. People cannot think in these millions. We must get down to business. If there are too many trains running we must discontinue some of them, if there are too many men employed for the work to be done, we must make necessary reductions. I have considered the facts as disclosed by the Minister of Railways. The hon member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) seems to think the only test that can be applied to discover what is wrong in the railway system is the amount of the operating expenditures. The actual test is the cost per ton train mile. We have not reached that point jn the argument and the figures have not been disclosed. The expense per train ton mile will doubtless show that the percentage of expenses this year are much greater than last year. If the tonnage has not gone up in proportion to the expenses but has rather gone down, then something must be wrong with the management, because if tonnage goes down and expenditure increases, it is obvious that we are employing too many men or spending too much money in the operation of the railways.
TMr. Currie.]

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope that hon. member will bring his remarks more closely to bear on the subject.

I shall do so, Mr. Speaker. I regret very much that the motion was not framed in wider terms, because I think there should be an open discussion in this House of the management of the railways. That, however, has not been done, and I can only say that I cannot see my way clear to vote for the resolution, and I think that any man of independent mind will reach the same conclusion.

I desire to go on record on the amendment of the leader of the Opposition. To my mind it serves no other purpose than to becloud the issue that faces the country to-day. Why is this resolution before the House? Public opinion, stirred up by the newspapers of the country in consequence of the statement delivered to the House by the Minister of Railways, is now in a frenzy of unrest. Is the motion a solution of the problem? Is it a cure, a remedy? What is the situation? We are actually controlling 17,000 miles of railway under government ownership, and when the Grand Trunk Railway system will have been acquired we shall own, 22,500 .miles, the greatest railway system in the world. When the Government of the day decided to go into the ownership of railways, it was on certain conditions and in the face of certain opposition. I for one have opposed public ownership. I believe that it is not sensible in view of the competition of privately owned companies. But there are some people in this country, as there are members in this House, who have faith in the principle of public ownership; and there is a Government that went on record as being confident in its soundness. Therefore it is the duty of members in this House to give to everyone who believes in public ownership an opportunity to prove whether or not it is feasible and profitable.

How long a time do you
require to prove that?

I am willing to discuss the railway situation whenever the question is under consideration. But I claim that the submission to this Parliament of every bit of correspondence, and every communication relative to the railways, will not provide a remedy for the situation. The evil is in connection with the management.

and you cannot eradicate it by any ventilation of all this correspondence in Parliament. You must have an up-to-date management; you must have supervision; you must have the strictest economy and the highest efficiency. You will not find this in Parliament; you will find it in the management which you will secure for the roads. And I hope that the Government of the day will be strong enough to give td all those who favour public ownership an opportunity to show whether it can be made a success or not. In taking that position I do so against my own opinion. But I believe in the rule of the majority. The majority has decided that we should undertake the experiment of public ownership. Then let the majority rule; let them have a chance to show whether or not public ownership will be profitable. Do not try to becloud the issue; do not try to stir up feeling against those people who believe in the theory. I say, give them a chance, and when the question of public ownership of railways is brought before the House, then everyone will be at liberty to suggest any remedy which, in his opinion, is capable of solving the problem which confronts Canada to-day.

If I rightly understood the remarks of the last speaker, the hon. member for St. Ilyacinthe, there may be some doubt as to his position on this question. He is in favour of private ownership; he does not favour public ownership; nevertheless, he is willing to change his opinion at the expense of the country.
No, no.
I rise to a point of order. The hon. member has no right to put into my mouth, for the purpose of bolstering up his argument, words which I never used.

The interpretation I have given the speech of my hon. friend I honestly base on my understanding of his remarks. The hon. gentleman said most explicitly that he did not believe in public ownership, but that nevertheless he was willing to alter his views-
Not at all.
I never made such a statement.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The rule is very clear, that if an hon. member makes a statement, it must be accepted by the House. On the other hand, however, it is quite competent for an hon. member to give his own interpretation of the remarks of any other member and base an argument thereupon. The remarks of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe will appear in Hansard and will stand as he stated them.

I do not want to be unjust in any way to the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe. He has delivered his speech and it is open to interpretation by every member of the House. Now, coming back to what I was saying. I say that the hon. gentleman declared that he was opposed to public ownership, but nevertheless would vote against this amendment so as to allow the Government to run the railways of this country in the way they have been running them for the last three years-and we know what results have attended that administration. The question before the House is much wider, broader, more general, than hon. members, including the member for St. Hyacinthe, have seen fit to consider it. The stand taken by the Opposition, Mr. Speaker, is that the Government of Canada -no matter whether it is a Liberal, a Tory, a Farmer or a Nationalist Government-cannot spend the public moneys of this country without rendering due account to the people's representatives. The amendment is not simply to be narrowed down to the railway issue in Canada-the issue is the very general one as to whether this Government is responsible to Parliament. The railway issue has been discussed. We might also discuss the matter of the Canadian Mercantile Marine; we might discuss every expenditure made by this Government for the last three or four years. The Opposition says to the Government: "If you wish to have money for the coming year then before these moneys are voted, you must do what every other Government in a constitutional country does-render proper accounts to the members of this House." This has not been done. Whenever information is sought, whenever information is demanded, the members of the Government-for some reason or other-have always refused to give us that information with respect to many matters of vital importance to the Canadian people.
Referring briefly to the side issue of railways, and putting aside the very general issue of the responsibility of the Government to the House of Commons, I say we have reached a stage in Canada where the railway situation has to be discussed openly, frankly and sincerely. I agree

with all the members who have spoken on either side, that the issue is so big, so vast, that it is not to be discussed in a partisan way. I, for one, do not intend to so discuss it. But the Government cannot run away from its own record, and the Government is responsible for the situation as it exists to-day. Who took over the Canadian Northern railway, who took over the Grand Trunk railway, who took over the Grand Trunk Pacific? This Government, or its predecessor; and the financial situation we are facing to-day is the direct result and consequence of the policy adopted by it. This is one fact that W cannot ignore. Another fact is that, in the light of the present unfavourable financial situation, if we had the facts put before the House, if the officials of all the public departments would give to us the information to which we are entitled, we would come to the conclusion that the East once more is paying for the West; and every business man in the eastern provinces is realizing to-day that on account of western demands they are facing a situation that cannot last much longer. I have not been surprised at the attitude taken by the Agrarian group on this question. It is in the interest of that group, it is in the interest of the western farmers at large, to see that the eastern people, or rather the population of the eastern provinces, do not realize exactly the liabilities and the obligations put on their shoulders by the situation that exists in the West. I do not wish to insist much longer on this phase of the question, but I say that it does not matter whether you belong to the Liberal party, whether you belong to the Tory party, or whether you belong to the Agrarian party-some day you will have to solve the whole financial and the whole railway problem in Canada. Then the eastern provinces will demand from the Government whether they are to continue paying,for the western provinces, and much will depend on the answer that shall be given. Those who say that this question should not be discussed from a political point of view are absolutely right. It must be discussed from a national point of view, and in the correct solution of the issue will be found the settlement of the question of our national unity in the future. The East has done very much for the West. The West has been built up by the East. And it seems, Mr. Speaker, that the East must continue to pay for the West, and the West will refuse to pay anything for the East. These are very 
grave questions and I think they should be discussed thoroughly, either before the House itself or before committees appointed for that purpose. I shall support the amendment presented by the leader of the Opposition because it embodies the high constitutional principle of parliamentary responsibility, and I say that this Government has no right to spend public moneys without giving to the representatives of the people that information to which they are entitled.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Will the hon. member
permit me a question? Does he contend that every amendment moved in this House, no matter what its terms, which becomes a motion of want of confidence must be supported. Irrespective, I say again, of its terms, by any who have not confidence in the general policy of the administration?

Mr. Speaker, with all
respect to my right hon. friend, I have been too long in this House, and I have crossed swords with him too often, to be drawn into any argument of that kind. If I were to remind the House to-day of the resemblance that the right hon. gentleman bears to the famous character pictured by Butler, it would not be the first time that I had done so, because on a former occasion I likened him to Hudibras of whom Butler said:
He could distinguish and divide
A hair twixt South and Southwest side.
Now, Sir, following your endeavours to keep hon. members to the amendment before the House, I desire to run over briefly some of the arguments that have been advanced in opposition to this amendment. As I have said, the only politics that has been introduced was introduced by the right hon. gentlemen himself. All that is said in this amendment is, that if you are going to discuss it from the standpoint of the Canadian National Railway system, then, as that system is a public undertaking, we, as the representatives of the people, are entitled to the fullest possible information regarding that undertaking. That is all this amendment says, and less than that we could not say if we are to discharge properly our trust to the public who send us here. Then, Sir, I object to the insinuation, no matter from what quarter it comes, that anybody on this side of the House, any more than any other hon. gentleman sitting in any other quarter of this chamber, is actuated by a desire to introduce politics or to discuss the merits or demerits of public
ownership. These questions do not enter into this amendment, and I decline to discuss them. The amendment should be discussed simply in accordance with the language in which it is expressed.
In his speech this afternoon my right hon. friend, following the example set by the hon. Minister of Railways a few days ago, invited expressions of opinion from hon. members on both sides of this House. That invitation we on this side have responded to, and when we do respond, the charge is made against us, either that we are opposed to public ownership, or that we are introducing politics. The invitation, Sir, I am bound to say could only relate, having regard to the language and attitude of my right hon. friend, to a discussion of the latter part of the amendment dealing with the Canadian National Railway system. But as pointed out by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) and by my hon. friend who sits to my right (Mr. Fielding) this amendment raises a much wider question than that. It goes to the whole root of responsible government, and it brings directly in issue the question of ministerial responsibility to a parliament representing what is supposed to be a free and democratic people. That is what this amendment is designed toJ bring before this chamber, and not what has been discussed by the majority of the hon. members who have spoken in opposition to the amendment.
Now, let me run over briefly some of the things that were said by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. In the course of his remarks he admitted that the Government was responsible for the success of the Canadian National system; but he said that they were not immediately accountable for day-to-day operation. Well, Sir, that may be useful perhaps as an admission, but it does not go to the root of the matter raised by this amendment, and the only observation that I desire to make upon it at the moment is that in view of what the right hon. Prime Minister admits, that the Government is being responsible for the success of the system, therefore the Government must also be responsible for the failure of the system-a failure that was put forth the other day by the Minister of Railways and Canals in terms that have staggered the whole Dominion.
Further, the right hon. gentleman said that if details of day-to-day operation were to be given the business of Parliament would he held up and made impossible. But here may I point out to the right hon. gentleman and to the House

that neither in the amendment itself, nor in the speech supporting it delivered by the hon. leader of the Opposition, was any specific method mentioned as to how this information, to which the representatives of the people are entitled, should be given to Parliament. That question was left entirely in the large, and I submit, Sir, that acceptance of the terms of this amendment would not at all have the effect which was foreshadowed by the right hon. Prime Minister.
Then the right hon. gentleman went on to point out that in his opinion, if information were brought down as requested by this amendment with reference to the Canadian National Railway system, that would operate to the injury of the Canadian National Railway system, for the reason that such information would become the property of its great competitor, the Canadian Pacific railway. Well, I have only to repeat what my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) and other hon. gentlemen have said, namely, that there is nothing done by the Canadian National Railway system or by its board or by any of those connected with its management that is not known within a very few hours to the management and directors of the Canadian Pacific railway. The Canadian Pacific railway is, as has been stated, one of the most successfully operated and best managed transportation systems in the world, and no amount of information that might be brought down in this House or before any committee of this House would add anything to the information of those who are charged with the. duty of managing and operating the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Therefore I dismiss that argument, and so will any practical business man, without any further consideration.
The right hon. gentleman also asked if the Canadian Pacific railway was shrouded in any mystery, and he answered his own question in the negative. That answer was correct. But then he added that neither was the Canadian National Railway system shrouded in any mystery. Well, that <s just exactly where we join issue with him. We say it is shrouded in mystery, and the proof of our assertion is that whenever information is asked for from this side of the House it is denied on the ground that it would not be in the public interest to bring that information down. That is where we say the shrouding in mystery comes in in regard to the Canadian National Railway system. But there is also another difference to be pointed out in this regard, namely that there is no necessity for

shrouding the Canadian Pacific railway in mystery. That road, as I have already said, is a successfully managed road and produces dividends; the reverse, according to the Minister of Railways and Canals, is the case with the Canadian National Railway system. And there is this further difference, that the Canadian Pacific railway, if it did make deficits, would not, as is the case with the Canadian National Railway system, come to this House from time to time	and ask the
representatives of the people to vote moneys to make up	those deficits.
Then the hon. gentleman proceeded and asked, what is to be done? I took down his exact words. He said: "If Parliament set to work through a committee of this House to evolve some rule that could be followed, it would evolve something definite and concrete." Now, Mr. Speaker, just mark that sentence, and at once you trace the resemblance to the historic character with whom I compared the right hon. gentleman a few moments ago. Let me read that again: "If Parliament set to work through a committee of this House to evolve some rule that could be followed, it would evolve something definite and concrete." In that you have the right hon. Prime Minister's solution of this whole railway question.
Then the right hon. gentleman expressed a preference for a committee-at least, he seemed to do so. I should not make any very definite statement with regard to anything my right hon. friend says or does; I have known him too long and too well to do that. But the right hon. gentleman, following the sentence that I have just quoted, seemed to indicate some interest in any event in the resolution which stands on the Order Paper in the name of the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) and intimated that if the committee provided for by that resolution were appointed, parties could be brought before it and all necessary information given there by officials connected, not only with the Canadian National Railway system, but with other roads as well.
