After Recess
The House resumed at Eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, just before you left the Chair at six o'clock, I had mentioned that the Prime Minister had based one of his objections to the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposi-

tion, on the fact that the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) had, standing in his name on the Order Paper, a motion providing for the appointment of another standing committee in addition to those already appointed by the House. The right hon. gentleman spoke in approving terms of the proposed new committee, and in the course of his observations with reference to it, he said that it might well be considered as likely to meet the situation raised by the amendment of the leader of the Opposition. That language evidently appealed to the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), as in the course of the remarks that he made following those of the Prime Minister, my hon. friend also expressed his approval of the creation of this new standing committee, and in answer to a question addressed to him by the leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Marquette said that he thought that any question could be asked and the answer could be obtained before this new standing committee. That reply seemed to me to be based on an erroneous idea of the scope and powers of a standing committee of this House. Lef me point out to my hon. friend in the first place that, when such a committee is appointed, it remains an inert thing; it does not function; it remains just so many names on a piece of paper until something is referred to it by this House for inquiry or investigation or report. Even when that has been done, in order that it may discharge the function which, it seems to me, the hon. member for Marquette had in mind it would perform as a matter of course, it must also receive from this House authority to send for persons, papers and records. Besides that, it must receive authority to examine witnesses under oath, and then under an Act it has "power to administer oaths to such witnesses. In order to accomplish what the hon. member for Marquette seemed to think this new committee would accomplish, all that I have mentioned would, in the first place, have to be done. In the next place, as I have stated, something would have to be referred to that committee, and in order to get the information that my hon. friend thought such a committee would get, the whole railway' situation as it affects the Canadian National Railway system at this time, would have to be referred to the committee and the committee would have to be invested with the powers and jurisdiction which I have just outlined before any information
worth having could be obtained. If the hon. member for Marquette can have that done, or if there is a possibility that such a thing would be done by the Government, I admit that the hon. gentleman would have some ground on which to base his argument. But if that is not done,-and I have very grave doubt that any such thing would be done,-with all respect I would point out to my hon. friend that his argument along that line and on that point proceeds from an error with regard to the facts.
Now, if such a committee were appointed, let me direct the attention of the House to the fact that my hon. friend and those who argue with him would then be impaled on either horn of another dilemma. My hon. friend, following the lead of the Prime Minister, had urged very strongly, against the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition, that in the getting of the information which they seemed to think would be got by the adoption of this amendment, information would be given to the great rival of the Canadian National Railway system, and that the giving of such information would operate to the injury of the government-owned and operated railway. If the suggestion of the hon. gentleman be followed, if this committee be appointed, and if this committee is not to be a body conducting its investigations after the manner of a star chamber, if this committee is to sit in public and to examine publicly persons, records and documents, then the information that will be elicited will be information, not only for the Canadian Pacific railway, but for all the world. So I ask my hon. friends who were urging against the amendment of the leader of the Opposition, the argument that to adopt it would mean the giving of information to the Canadian Pacific how they are going to get away from the greater volume of information that would be given by holding sessions of such a committee as that. They are impaled on either horn of that dilemma, and I leave the hon. gentlemen to select which of those horns they prefer.
Let me deal with this matter very briefly from another and, perhaps, a more important point of view. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid), a few days ago, and the Prime Minister this afternoon, invited discussion and suggestions, and hon. members who spoke from this side, and, indeed, from all quarters of the House, expressed their willingness to ac-

cept the invitation and to give such assistance in the solution of the railway difficulties that confront us as they would, in the exercise of their best judgment and their greatest diligence, be able to give. Some doubt was cast, without any reason whatever, upon the bona-fides of statements of that kind emanating from the Opposition. Without going into that, let me point out that in order to discuss a thing, you must know what that thing is. If we are to discuss the railway situation, we must know all the facts that produced that situation. If we are to discuss the conditions which have brought about the situation with which the country is confronted to-day, and for being the cause of which I, in any * event would not think of blaming hon. gentlemen who now sit opposite-if, we are to discuss that situation and if we are to suggest the remedies which, in our judgment, should be applied, to change that situation, to put an end to those huge deficits and to put the railway system, owned and operated by the Government, on a proper basis, surely it is elementary that before we can do that, we must have before us the facts relating to the whole situation.
Let me point out a few things bearing on the proposition which I have just laid down and which, I submit, cannot be successfully refuted. On the 14th of the present month, the gentleman who at present occupies the position of chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners of Canada delivered a speech before a club in this city. I refer to the Hon. F. B. Carvell, whose speech on the occasion to which I have referred attracted nation-wide attention. In order that I may not transgress the rules of the House, and for the purpose of keeping strictly to the amendment that is now before us for discussion, I will quote just two sentences of the speech as bearing on the subject at issue. In the Ottawa Journal of March 15, there appears a report of the speech in question, and Mr. Carvell is represented as having made these statements:	[DOT]
The Government railway losses last year were far greater than recently reported. They are \ery much more than what has appeared on the surface.
I am not going to comment upon those statements, but I am going to draw the attention of the House to what was said a day or two later by one of the leading journals^ in this country with reference to those statements. In the Toronto Globe of the 17th instant, there appears an editorial, the title of which is "Are these charges

true"? Ag'ain, in order to confine myself strictly to the amendment, I will read just those portions of the editorial which bear upon the matter which we are discussing. In the course of that article the Globe said, referring to the statements which I have just cited as being made by Mr. Carvell:
If words mean anything, Mr. Carvell charges the board of management of the Canadian National railways or the Minister of Railways, or both, with making false representations as to the condition of the people's railways. The losses, he asserts, are very much more than what has appeared on the surface. Is Dr. Reid content to let this imputation of deceit and concealment rest upon him?
Those are not my words, nor do I associate myself with them at the moment. Later on in the editorial there are these further observations:
Are the figures false, and presented to Parliament with the intent to deceive? If they are, Mr. Carvell will do the people of Canada a service by stating wherein they are untrue.
These are the comments of one of the leading newspapers of Canada upon that portion of the speech of the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners to which I have just drawn the attention of the House. Certainly no more serious comment could be made upon that statement than those that are made in that editorial of the Globe, and if for no other reason than to place himself right, my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals, and the Government of which he is a member, should, I submit, welcome the earliest possible opportunity, and any method that offers itself, to place all available information before' the public so as to disprove the gravity of the charges contained in the speech delivered by Mr. Carvell.
Now, the speech itself was not alone the only serious statement that went forth to the Canadian public. A statement made in this House a day or two later by the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals, in disclosing the railway situation as it exists in Canada at the present time, has stirred several journals supporting the Government to give expression to their views in very plain terms. I am not going to quote from them at any great length, nor in fact will I refer to any but one, and in doing so I will again confine myself to that part of the article which is germane to the subject under discussion.
The Ottawa Journal in its issue of the 15th instant, in referring to the disclosures made by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals in this House in presenting the statement to which I have alluded, said this:

The people appear willing to assume the burden, and that attitude would justify the utmost frankness upon the part of the Minister of Railways. At the moment they are asking for full information as to the exact volume of the burden involved, and that is a reasonable desire. The burden itself neither swells nor shrinks under the light of truth. To say that ''this total does not include fixed charges on the Intercolonial and the National Transcontinental" falls short of meeting the popular desire for information in a spirit of perfeot candor.
That language, Mr. Speaker, is not the language of a Liberal. That language is not the language of any hon. member sitting on this side of the House. That language, Sir, is not the language of an opponent of this Government. That language is the language of a journal than which there is no stronger supporter of the present Government in the whole Dominion of Canada, and surely, Sir, the Government will take notice of this statement of the Journal, speaking of the people that- "At the moment they are asking for full information as to the exact volume of the burden involved, and that is a reasonable desire." Mr. Speaker, that language applies aptly to the terms of the amendment introduced by the hon. the leader of the Opposition, and in support of which I am citing this editorial for the information of this House. Then how true it is as the Journal states further: "The burden itself neither swells nor shrinks under the light of truth." And how well deserved this reproof is in the concluding part of the extract in which the language used by the minister is quoted, when the . Journal observes: "To say that 'this total does not include fixed charges on the Intercolonial and the National Transcontinental' falls short of meeting the popular desire for information in a spirit of perfect candor." Now, Sir, I submit that from this source, from this newspaper favourable to the * Government, comes the very strongest en-dorsation of the position taken by the hon. the leader of the Opposition in his amendment.
But, Sir, there are a couple of other incidents that illustrate the need for information to which I might with propriety allude before I resume my seat. Occasionally we do get some information from the Government, but no sooner do we get it than one of two things happens: either it is pointed out the next day that the information is erroneous, or, as happened with reference to two statements made by the Government on different occasions, there is such a direct conflict of fact that further information is absolutely necessary.
Now, to illustrate the first point, I need only remind the House that a short time ago my hon. friend, the Minister of Railways and Canals, in replying to a question asked by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) with regard to the number of locomotives built by the Montreal Locomotive company for this Government since the year 1917, and replying to a further question as to the value of these locomotives, gave an answer to the House one day saying that the value was $1,300,000 odd. On that day he also stated that his colleague, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, was a director of the locomotive company which manufactured these locomotives. Then, Sir, on the following day, my hon. friend, the Minister of Railways and Canals, rose in his seat and corrected the figures that had been given to him to present to the House the previous day, and said that the value of the locomotives built by this company since the year 1917, this company of which his colleague, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, is a director, instead of being $1,300,000 odd was thirteen millions and some odd thousand dollars. Now, Mr. Speaker, in the light of errors of that kind in information furnished by the Government itself, and directly bearing on the railway situation in this country, surely we are entitled to the fullest possible information as to the whole series of contracts given this locomotive company,-as to the type and size of locomotives they built, as to the comparison of costs between these locomotives when built by that company and the same locomotives when built by any other company. Further, I submit, we are entitled to another comparison, a comparison of the cost of these locomotives, and locomotives of the same type and size when built for a private-owned and privately operated company. [DOT] Further than that, we are entitled,
I also submit, to this additional information: we ought to know how much locomotives of the same type and size cost in the United States as compared with the cost in Canada.
I am only citing these as one branch, and * a very small branch, of the inquiry that ought to be made and of the information that ought to be given before any hon. gentleman^ in this House or any citizen of this country can intelligently approach the discussion of what is generally referred to as the present railway situation.
One other illustration and I have done. At the time the Estimates were brought down in this House a statement was given

to the newspapers by the Government in explanation of the appalling state of affairs disclosed by these Estimates. In that statement reference was made to the amount of operating loss, and the amount that was then mentioned was a few days later proved to be quite incorrect and much below the actual figure when the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals made his official statement in this House. This incident, illustrating the unreliability of the figures given to this House, and illustrating further, the fact that the hon. the Minister of Railways apparently cannot depend upon those who are responsible for furnishing him with this information was dealt with in a communication to the Montreal Star, from which I intend to quote a few sentences. The Star has begun the publication of a series of articles on the railway situation contributed by Mr. J. L. Payne, a gentleman who under this and former Governments occupied the position of Chief Railway Statistician for the Dominion of Canada. The first of these letters appeared in the Star of Saturday last, and a supplementary letter was published yesterday. In this supplementary letter Mr. Payne makes reference to the discrepancy to which I have just alluded, in the following terms:
The newspaper figuresthat is to say, those handed out by the Government concurrently with the introduction of the Estimates in this House.
-had placed the operating loss at $21,250,000 fiom which I deduct 5,000,000 on account of probable net operating earnings by the Grand Trunk; but Dr. Reid showed that the loss for the past year from operation had been $36,842,-S' 0.17. To the extent of the difference between $21,250,000 and that sum, the deficit for the current year may be taken as having been Inc-eased.
So that whether we are denied information, or whether we get information which is immediately afterwards proven to be incorrect, it is quite evident that neither we in this House, nor the citizens of the country at large, are in a position even to approach the discussion of the railway situation until there is available a far greater volume of information than that which we and the people now possess, and until that information is obtained through sources upon which we may rely as being absolutely correct.
My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), in discussing the amendment presented by the leader of the Opposition, took exceptions to it upon two grounds. In the first place, he said it was prema-

ture; and besides that, he contended that it was not supported by information which we should have had before the amendment was introduced. Well now, I submit to my hon. friend that not only is this amendment not premature, but that the time has arrived-indeed that the time has passed- when this House should take a stand, such as that proposed by the amendment, to assert its rights and privileges with regard to information to which members of Parliament are entitled as representatives of the people of Canada. I cannot for a moment admit, therefore, that the amendment is at all premature. As regards the argument that the amendment is not supported by information which we should have had before it was brought forward,
I	confess that I do not quite understand this contention of my hon. friend. It is quite unlike him. He is usually remarkable, not only for clarity of speech, but also for clarity of thought. But without labouring that point, may I draw his attention and the attention of the House to the fact that his objection is baseless. He says that the amendment should be supported by information which we ought to have had before it was brought into the House. Well, Sir, we tried to get information and were refused it, and to-day we are seeking the very thing which the hon. member says we should have got. From that point of view, therefore, I invite my hon. friend to revise the opinion he expressed this afternoon, and to be logical, as he usually is, by voting with the members of the Opposition in suport of the amendment.

The question involved in the amendment of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) is not without difficulties, and I desire to say a word or two thereon before voting upon the question. Notwithstanding your very excellent voice, Mr. Speaker, which usually covers this chamber to the satisfaction of every hon. member, I am sure it is not to be presumed, upon a single reading of a motion, that it has been clearly followed by hon. gentlemen, and I should like to read the amendment again for my own satisfaction, and possibly for the information of the House. It is as follows:
That subject to the reservation that in exceptional cases there may be documents of a c mfidential character which, in the public interest, may properly be withheld from publication ; the House declares that It is the undoubted right of Parliament to demand and receive copies of all reports, accounts, correspondence and papers in relation to the management of

every department of the public service, including the affairs of the Canadian National railways, whether operating directly under the control of a department or under corporate form.
After a reading of that resolution, and a careful observance of the text, it may be that hon. gentlemen are not far apart, even accepting the views already expressed to-day as being the judgment of the House generally. The amendment uses the term "confidential," which is the qualifying portion of the resolution; and I think it of some importance to inquire just for a moment as to what that word means. I assume that the leader of the Opposition, in incorporating that term into his amendment, did not wish thereby to imply that the only documents that were to be withheld from Parliament were those merely ' which had been marked "confidential" by the writer, or which had been so considered by the recipient of the letter. I assume- in fact I hope-that he did not intend to use the word in that restrictive sense. I should think that he meant that if the Government considered that any special document asked for by Parliament should not be disclosed to the House or to the public, because it was against the public interest, therefore it would be a confidential document. If I unfairly interpret the hon. gentleman's use of that particular word I trust he will correct me. The Canadian National Railways, of which the people of Canada are the shareholders, is a business institution and, as has been pointed out by several speakers during the course of the debate, it has its competitors. As every hon. gentleman knows, there is in all business affairs a great deal that cannot be divulged to the public. This, I think, is regarded as a safe principle which is always followed by corporations and their shareholders, who usually protest against the disclosure of facts to the public, except through the medium of shareholders' meetings. This principle is regarded by private individuals as a sound one, and it is one that is usually observed. Therefore, when I say that in all business affairs there is much that is confidential and must not be disclosed to the public. I think I am stating what is axiomatic and which will be accepted by every hon. gentleman in the House. If I am right in my interpretation of the qualifying section of the amendment I would say that if upon a motion for documents, the Government believe that disclosure or publication of the same would be against the national interests, would be
against the interests of the Canadian National Railway system, they would refuse to divulge or publish the same on that ground and therefore those documents would be regarded as confidential. It is true that the Government must take the responsibility of determining what information shall be given to the public, what documents relative to the administration of the Canadian National railway system shall be divulged. It may be that the opponents of the Government might differ from them in their view as to what was confidential and what was not confidential, as to what information should be divulged and what should be maintained as purely for the guidance of those interested. In that event Parliament would have to judge as to who was right and who was wrong; and ultimately it would be the right and duty of the public, who are the proprietors of the railway system, to determine as to whose position was correct-that of the Government or that of their opponents. If my interpretation of the amendment of the leader of the Opposition is correct-and it does seem the proper one, it does seem the natural and obvious interpretation

so far as I am concerned I cannot see any objection to it. It expresses a principle which it seems to me would be very dangerous for this Parliament to oppose or to deny. After all, it is within the power of the Government to determine what information they judge to be in the public interest to divulge and what they deem not proper to divulge. I therefore fail to see upon what principle the amendment should be denied by the House.
I should be reluctant to oppose the amendment upon another ground. A few days ago the Minister of Railways presented his annual statement upon the railways owned and controlled by the Government, and I think the statement as to form was a very excellent one. Upon reading it, subsequent to its deliverance, I find that not only is it in splendid form, but it gives a very great deal of information. The minister stated there would be a deficit of $70,000,000 this year in operating and fixed charges. He also estimates that for the current year there will be a deficit of $50,000,000 for operating and fixed charges. When one reflects upon the world-wide conditions to-day, when one recalls the commercial and financial conditions in all the leading countries of the world, he might be pardoned if he did say that the deficit in the current year would probably be as large as it was last year. Now this deficit, Mr. Speaker, must be made up by the people of

Canada in the form of taxation. There is no royal road by which we can secure that amount of money to square the accounts of the Canadian National Railway system, except by obtaining it through taxation upon the people of the Dominion.

We might
save on the railroads.

That would lessen the amount to be taken from the people by taxation, but the principle would not be varied by the difference in amount. It being true that this enormous deficit must be made up through taxation from the people I, at least, shall be very reluctant to give adherence to the principle that Parliament must not, in the general sense at any rate, be afforded the fullest information that it deems necessary in connection with the operation of that railway system and which goes to make up a deficit for which the people have to be taxed. It is quite true that a great deal of information might well be denied Parliament and the public by the Government and by the management of the railway system, but speaking in the general sense, I say, they are entitled to all information. The exceptions can only be determined as the cases arise, and when they come before us in a concrete form. Then, and only then, I submit can we determine what information should be refused the public and Parliament by the Government and by the management of the railways, and all one can do at the present time is to either affirm or deny the. general principle embodied in the amendment which is now before us for consideration. Very much has been said this afternoon in connection with the operation of the National railway system that is commendable. For the present at least we are the proprietors of these railways, the mileage of which will be enlarged when the Grand Trunk system is acquired. It does not follow from my remarks, or from the fact that we are the proprietors of this National railway system, that members of Parliament should ask all sorts of questions, and move for the production of all sorts of documents, without discretion and without discrimination. Many questions are asked, I think, which are not informative to anybody, which are not perhaps in the national interest, and which are not perhaps in the interest of the railway system itself. I admit, Sir, it is sometimes difficult to determine, as a matter of fact, what questions are relevant, what are important, what are informative,
[Mr. Maclean.!
and what are or are not in the national interest. The answers to some questions, it has been suggested by some hon. gentleman this afternoon, may be quite satisfying to curious and inquisitive people outside of Parliament, but it does not necessarily follow that it is in the public interest that such questions should be asked, and only questions that are in the public interest should be asked. Nor does it follow that because some persons, whom some of us in this House represent, desire questions to be asked, the time of Parliament should be taken up either in the asking or in the answering of them. It was inevitable, Mr. Speaker, that the issue involved in this motion should have arisen. I assume that every hon. member felt that when the policy of government ownership and control was adopted, this very issue was bound to be projected into Parliament. It is one of the difficulties incident to and inherent in Government ownership, and we must make the best of it. It may be true that the privilege of asking questions and demanding the production of documents has not up to the present been abused. I am hardly in a position to state that it has been. Probably we will acquire a better standard as to what should be required in this connection by having no rule whatever rather than attempting to regulate it by standing orders or by rules. But I am sure we will all agree that having accepted the tremendous responsibility of becoming the owners and operators of 17,000 or 18,000 miles of railway, that railway should be given a fair trial, and it should not in any way be prejudiced by the attitude taken by hon. gentlemen.
Now I have admitted, Mr. Speaker, that Parliament is entitled to a great deal of information. If the people are to be taxed to meet large deficits in future, as they will be, it naturally follows that they will expect a great deal of information from Parliament. But while the people and Parliament are entitled to this infdrmation, still we should contrive some method by which such information should reach Parliament and the people other than through the Order Paper or the ordinary channels. Refe'rence has been made to my motion now upon the Order Paper asking for the establishment of a standing committee upon Government-owned railways and shipping. I am not going to discuss that motion, but I propose to debate it at the earliest opportunity. I might say, however, that one of the reasons which moved me to place that motion upon the Order Paper was the hope

that this committee would work out some method by which Parliament and the people might be kept better informed in future on railway affairs. I also entertained the hope that some regulations or standing orders might be set up which would in some way control the means by which Parliament and [DOT] the people would be kept informed, thus saving much of the time of Parliament.
In connection with our railway questions,
I think I am uttering but the simple truth when I say that Parliament and the people require information. During the past fifteen or twenty years, at least during the time that I have been a member of this House, it seems to me, reflecting on the years that have gone by, that Parliament has abdicated its functions, particularly in relation to railway matters. We were not informed thereon, and it would appear that we did not take care always to be informed; too blindly did we follow the Government's view of or perhaps some section of [DOT] public opinion. But I submit that we have reached the time when Parliament should become informed upon this great national issue, in which is involved a problem that will confront us for many years to come. In the absence, however, of an alternative method of informing Parliament upon that problem and of dealing with the very issue raised in this amendment, I think the amendment does contain a principle which should be affirmed, though in practice it should perhaps be strictly qualified, and therefore I propose to support it.

Mr. Speaker, without attempting to throw blame on any one in particular, the thought strikes me that it would have been better in so far as the aim of the discussion was to really accomplish something which would be profitable in the way of understanding the present railway situation, and, after understanding it, to take measures to improve it, had a more opportune moment been chosen when the discussion would have been placed upon a somewhat wider plane and would, I think, have issued in better results. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) knew very well that the motion which was placed on the Order Paper by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) would probably be reached within a day. Why was it necessary then, by injecting a motion in amendment to the Government's motion to go into Supply, to bring up the question on a narrow basis, rather than approach it as a whole House from both sides in the
only proper spirit in which it can be approached-an entire .negation of any desire to make party capital on one side or the other, and a full purpose in a very solemn and a very careful way to front the problem than which no more important problem has been before the Parliament of Canada since Confederation? If there is anything that should make a parliament sober and earnest and honest with itself, it is a situation such as that which confronts us to-day.
I do not think that men on this side or men on that side of the House, if they are going to arrive at a proper solution of this problem, have any time to waste in throwing boquets one at the other as to who was the way-back cause of the present situation. I think it should make some of us very humble in our criticisms if we let our memories go back to the antecedent times during which the bases were formed which have eventuated in the situation confronting us to-day. I for one do not propose to go into ancient history as to which particular party or government was in part or in whole to blame. The fact is that we have a very serious proposition before us upon which the economic and financial and national progress depends in a very essential way.
That is my view of the situation and the way in which we should approach it, and my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition does not appear to me to have taken the best course in the light of that broad, general interest by interjecting this amendment on the motion to go into Supply. He will take my criticism as a kindly criticism. I could have hoped that we should have been spared this and should have come to the discusion of the situation on broad, general lines.
My hon. friend, the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), has endeavoured to define the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition. I tried to follow his definition, and it seemed to me that he took about three different positions in that regard. I followed him sympathetically in the first; I then had to reverse the engine and follow him sympathetically in the second, and so with the third, and I got confused and troubled about it. I think I shall have to have some further light from my hon. friend before I can exactly see the point towards which he was going. My hon. friend who leads the Opposition knows the English language and the meaning of its words; he knows not only the colloquial meaning but also

the official meaning of the word "confidential." Looking thro.ugh his vocabulary, without having to go to the dictionary- because I am sure he has a vast choice of words-my hon. friend chose that one word "confidential," and put it into his motion, and it is an essential part of that motion. If the word "confidential" meant what the member for Halifax read as its meaning in his first interpretation of it, the leader of the Opposition would have been just as well up in business, just as far up in the line, if instead of putting into his motion something about confidential information he had incorporated in it the affirmation that as a rule the sun rises every morning and sets every night-a self-evident truth. If "confidential" means what the member for Halifax had in mind, what kind of information will my hon. friend get, and those who vote for his amendment, if the amendment carries? Exactly the information which the Government chooses to give him in the light of the public interest and no more.
Talking about the privileges of the House and the different disposition of, powers of government and claims of justice to members of Parliament, has anybody ever taken the position that as this chamber votes the money, so this chamber has the right to know to the last dollar how it has been expended? I have not heard that position taken in this House, but if it is true, it is equally true that a government is a mere automaton and has neither the right nor the power of existence in fact if it does not face every now and then the question as to what information it is in the public interest that it should give out. If the Government thinks it is not in the public interest that information should be given at a certain time or on a certain line, it is not only the right but the absolute duty of that government to withhold the information. One principle is just as necessary in government as the other; one is just as strongly entrenched in the constitution and in the general division of powers as the other. So that I would like to know the answer of my hon. friend the leader of [DOT]the Opposition as to his coincidence with interpretation number one given by the senior member for Halifax. Is that the meaning of his resolution? If it is, my hon. friend from Halifax will vote for it; if it is not, can he vote for it? There ought to be some finality about this, or a vote may go astray. To some members of Parliament it does not matter much whether a vote goes astray or not, but for either the leader of the Opposition or my hon. friend

from Halifax to have a vote go astray is a matter of some importance. Will these two gentlemen please settle between themselves what is the meaning of the word " confidential " and so inform us? We shall gain a vote or we shall lose a vote according as there is agreement or otherwise between them.
Let us look at it a little further. Two kinds of confidential documents are envisaged by my hon. friend; not all confidential documents are to be withheld by the Government, but only that division of confidential documents which it would be against the public interest to bring down. All other confidential ones are to be brought down. We must keep that ih mind: only those documents are to be refused the production of which would not be in the public interest. In a word, "confidential" having its general meaning and its special meaning, if the amendment is carried and becomes imperative, you will leave as it is now, in the discretion of the Government, the decision in all special cases whether a paper or document may or may not in the public interest be brought down, and you will have a standing battle between the Government and the Opposition or the seeker of the information on the question whether the Government is right in its interpretation or whether it is assuming autocratic or plenary powers and exercising great liberty in the production of information asked for. What I want to make plain is this: if the leader of the Opposition confines himself to confidential documents you will have to proceed then upon the division, first, into confidential documents the bringing down of which would not be prejudicial to the public interest and, second, confidential documents the bringing down of which would be prejudicial to the public interest. How will my hon. friend find those confidential documents? In a government department you find them easily. The minister or officer who indites a document or a letter marks it "confidential" or does not so mark it; if he marks it "confidential" he puts a seal upon it and it remains in that category. But in the case of a person or a corporation or a railway company carrying on business, how many of the documents or letters, how much of the correspondence, how many of the 9 p.m. transactions, are initialled as confidential by the only one who can initial them as such? Not one per cent of them, I venture to say. So that if my hon. friend's amendment passes he will be able to ask for nearly every document, every

item of correspondence which exists in connection with the administration of a great railway. I think there is no getting away from that. Well, when it comes to that I think we are up against a very important problem.
My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) got a little excited this afternoon, I think, and used naughty words

very naughty words for a man of his age and wisdom, but they got the better of him this afternoon, for a moment, and he used them. He used the word "autocracy" and threw it at us with very great vim and very great energy. He then used the "dark lantern" illustration, as if we were a band of professional burglars in this respect and were going around with dark lanterns looking for our neighbours' goods to appropriate them to our own advantage. There is no need of using hard words when you come to the contemplation or discussion of a question as important as this. But the fact that they were used just illustrates! my objection of a few moments ago that the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) got off the broad road of facing a great situation and discussing it in a cool and deliberate manner, and got on to the little, narrow road, not the narrow road which the Bible deals with, but the little, narrow road which is known to party politics, and he slid along it with more than his accustomed celerity and quickness. He would not have used those words if he had come up to the discussion of the question in a broad general way. But the words "autocracy" and "dark lantern" do not lend weight to an argument; they rather mark a divergence from the path along which you proceed to a reasoned and cool discussion of a subject, to the narrow path of which I spoke where you approach the subject from traditions of partyism and from tendencies towards partyism.
But that is not the way in which we will settle this question. My hon. friend compared a public department with the operations of a great railway system under corporate management. My hon. friend, if he comes to think of that for a minute, will see that there is no parallel between those two. The Department of Public Works is not in competition with any other agencies, private or corporate or public, along the same line of work. I.t receives a certain amount of money from this House; it has indicated what it wants that money for; it is for the public service, and this House has a right to the last dollar to have an
explanation of that expenditure, and the Public Works Department within its own domain, is engaged simply upon the outlined, delineated public services which this House authorizes it to carry on. How the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's could, for a moment, be led into the assertion that there was a parallel between the Department of Public Works and a great piece of enginery for the administration of eighteen or twenty thousand miles of railway in this country, I cannot understand; but the House can easily see that those are not parallel. While I agree with him up to the last in his assertion that the House has a right to have a full explanation of all those departmental expenditures, and that it must have them; when it comes to the other point, there are big interests upon which we have embarked; we have made a decision, that after these roads came to us-and they came to us; they pressed themselves upon us; they were taken in hand-they should not be carried on by government agency; that they should be in the form of corporate management, and we thereby divested ourselves of their direct management. Someone, with the usual lack of thought which the best of us sometimes may suffer from, has made the assertion that this great system of railways, as it exists today, is nothing more nor less than a party political machine. I am quite sure that the horn member who made that assertion did not quite think how far it went. Is it a party political machine? Has it been so used? Is it a hot-bed of patronage? I quite understand what patronage means, and I have my friends behind me-
Oh, oh.
24,000 census enumera-. tors.
The very mention of the word "patronage" puts joy on the faces of hon. gentlemen opposite.
We like to hear the admission.

When we refer to patronage, oh, joy, joy!-hon. gentlemen opposite are thinking of the time when they will hold the reins of power. That is why we hear such cheers and clapping from the other side of the House whenever the word "patronage" is used. It is like a sweet morsel that they roll under the tongue, of infinite gratification tq them. Do they want to come in and have its trials



as well as its joys? I know what patronage means.	-
Oh, oh.

From the time that the Intercolonial and the Canadian Northern shortly afterwards went out from the line of patronage, I have seen, and I have lived partly, in a different atmosphere. From the time that the new organization took hold, although I have been sometimes asked to get this man and that man and the other man a place within the administrative staff of that railway, I have never succeeded in doing so and I have never attempted to do so. There is no man, either outside of the ranks of those administrative officers or inside of them, that can controvert that statement with reference to myself. What does that prove? It proves that the Government, having laid down its policy, divested itself from the patronage in connection with the railways and held the management liable for the administration, the appointment of its staff, the promotion of its men and the general working out of the system. I have never interfered, and I think what is the fact as stated by myself would be the fact as stated by my colleagues as well. I will tell the House what I have heard. I have heard a good many pretty bitter remonstrances that in the old times it was possible to apply to a minister and get a man into a position, but now since the administration has been changed, that period has passed away and no one can seemingly get in by that path. But for a man to make in this House the statement that the whole of it is simply under a political patronage system and being run in that way, marks him, I am afraid, as a little bit thoughtless or a little bit reckless, whichever he may take as being the softest epithet to apply to himself.
I think I have stated all that it is necessary for me to state. There is but one thing more, and this bears out what the right hon. gentleman who leads the party has stated. I think that we members of Parliament, on both sides of the House should get as closely together and as quickly together as we possibly can, and try to find a solution for the situation which lies immediately in front of us. I think our reputation as members of Parliament depends upon that. I think that the country is looking to see Parliament come to some solution of that kind. They send their representatives to Parliament, those representatives are paid their emolument in Par- .
DSir George Foster.]
liament, and are supposed to do their duty in Parliament, and I submit that it is the duty of this Parliament and suceeeeding Parliaments to let bygones be bygones and partyism be partyism in the past, to be resumed in some dim and distant day in the future, if it is ever resumed, and for the time being to approach at least this one question with a sincere desire not to bother any one, but to get at the roots of the question-better still, to get at some sensible, sane method for solving the problem. We will not solve it by declamation nor by chucking words one at the other, whether it be "dark lanterns," "autocrats" or anything of that kind. We have enough brain, good will, and business ability in this Parliament to settle upon a solution which, though it must be gradual, will be effectual and pull us out. I agree with the sentiment uttered by my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark). I am not pessimistic enough to think that Canada, with her future prospects, cannot draw herself out from this difficult railway situation of today and, with courage, persistence, and hopefulness, carry on and carry through for one, two, three, maybe several years more, until the development of the country comes even with the splendid facilities of transport that we have provided for it, and when, as a consequence, the revenues of these roads will approach the supporting point and some day or other pass it and perhaps become feeders of our revenues. But we will not get to that situation without the most careful thought and without a union of effort mental and moral, of both parties and both sides of the House towards obtaining the solution of one of the most important questions that ever devolved upon a parliament.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria) :
speechtext:
I had not intended to take part in this debate, but the temptation to participate in a discussion which has been honoured by the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) taking a part in it. is perhaps a little too strong for me to resist. I wish to make a few observations on the motion before the House, and possibly a few remarks upon the speech which has just been made by the right hon. gentleman.
Ever since I have had anything to do with public speaking either in this House or out of it, I have always tried to cull some material from the speech of the man who. was talking against me, to use in my own speech. I have listened to the speech . of the right hon. gentleman with all the

attention I could bring to bear for material, but-and I say this with all respect-beyond hurling half a dozen dictionaries across the floor I know of nothing substantial that the right hon. gentleman has said. He was very much bothered about the definition of "confidential"; that word bothered him very much. He almost committed himself, however, to this, that if we on this side of the House agreed upon what " confidential " meant, and if it was the same as the amendment, possibly he would vote for it. I am prepared to tell the right hon. gentleman that those of us who have been in this House for the last sixteen or twenty years know what the practice of Liberal and Conservative governments have been in respect to withholding matters that they considered confidential, and bringing down matters that they did not deem confidential. In the seventeen years I have been in this House I never heard of a motion from either side, Liberal or Conservative, finding fault with any government or minister for having to refuse to bring down documents on the ground that they were confidential and that the bringing of them down was not in the best interest of the country. It was always left to the judgment of the minister and the Government as to whether or not they should be brought down. There might perhaps be a little fault finding but never within my memory has there been any motion censuring a government or minister for deeming such and such matters to be confidential.
There is not the slightest question about what is meant by this motion. The motion allows for the exercise of discretion on the part of the Government as to what shall be deemed confidential, and therefore to be withheld. That certainly was the purpose of the language of the motion; otherwise, it would have had no meaning at all. I absolutely agree with the definition given by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), who called upon the leader of the Opposition to correct him if he did not agree with him. There was no correction and the hon. gentleman went on with his speech. Consequently, I submit to the right hon. gentleman that the leader of the Opposition agreed with the position taken by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) and that the amendment as put forward bears the meaning and intent which the senior member for Halifax puts upon it. That being the case, I will call upon the right hon. gentleman to support this amendment, and to
advise his friends to support it, because according to the view I take, it is left largely, if not altogether, to the Government as to what shall and shall not be brought down.
The attitude that some wise men take is peculiar. The right hon. gentleman says that this amendment is premature. He says that we should not move this amendment until we have the information. Suppose we had not moved it until we had information. Then he would have said we were ridiculous for moving for information which we then possessed. What shall we do with gentlemen of that kind? We are moving for this information at the psychological moment, as my right hon. friend would say. How could we move for information of this kind except on a motion for the House to go into Committee of Supply? What is the object of this rule, which obtains both in Great Britain and here, that there must be a motion made before Mr. Speaker leaves the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Supply? This House goes into Committee of the Whole on public and private Bills and a host of other Bills, but it is only in the case of the House going into Committee of Supply that a motion must be made that the Speaker do leave the Chair. Why is that? Because the Government are coming to the House and asking for the expenditure of the people's money, and it is the right of the House to say whether or not they have put themselves in such a position as justifies the granting of that money. Now, the idea of this amendment is that the whole circumstances in connection with the expenditure of moneys in the Railway Department shall be thrashed out. I am here representing a certain number of people, and when I go back to my constituency, they will naturally be anxious to know something about this $70,000,000 deficit in connection with the Government Railways. I shall say that I do not know, that we were just told there was a lump sum, and, having asked the Prime Minister for information, were informed that it was not in the interests of the country that we should have that information, the railways being under the control of some incorporated company, and that we should therefore refrain from asking anything about them. Well-this is what my constituents will say-did you ask anyone else for information? Yes, I will reply; we asked the Minister of Railways, but he just parroted out the same words as uttered by the Prime Minister, to the effect that it was not in

the public welfare that the people should be told anything about the railways. My electors, if we did not introduce such an amendment as this, would then want to know why we voted for the expenditure of these moneys in the blind way in which this House is called upon to do. Why should the House be expected to play "blind man's buff" in matters of this kind? Why, Sir, seventy or eighty millions of the people's money is at stake, and we desire to be able to tell the electors that we did all we could to induce the Government to submit the facts, dividing the House upon the question, even though there might be a majority on the other side to vote us down. This is the kind of Government we have to-day, in the face of the situation with which we now have to deal; and my right hon. friend finds fault with the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), because that gentleman in his opinion, uses strong words! I do not quite understand this Sunday school simplicity of my right hon. friend.
A simple mind.

From the superficial knowledge which we can gather of this Government, it is not only hard words that they need. They need that instrument which a better man than the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's made use of; someone should take hold of the cord and whip them out of their seats. That is what should be done, and my right hon. friend should be thankful that he has not been brought into contact with some more material, more drastic and more painful instrument of persuasion than mere words and allusions to dark lanterns. Now, we are told by the Prime Minister, in his most solicitous and attractive tones, that he is very anxious to give us information. He wants to tell us everything about the expenditure of moneys in connection with the railways, but the Department of Railways is not to be trusted; we cannot get it through that department. But, he says, the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has found a remedy for all these evils; he is going to appoint another fifth wheel to the coach and add to the many standing committees we have now. He is going to appoint a standing committee before which-says my right hon. friend-you shall go and drink in abundantly all the information you require to your heart's content, and the public will know nothing about the matter. Did anyone ever hear a more childish proposition than that? I have been attending committees in this House for the last

17 or 18 years, and, Mr. Speaker, I never saw a committee sitting behind closed doors. I never saw a committee on any business of importance where we did not have, rail-birds all around us, representing every newspaper in' the country, gobbling up every sentence worth hearing. Does the right hon. gentleman think that when this great carcase is produced and thrown into open daylight, these same rail-birds will not again be on the scene? I think he is presuming too much if he thinks that their curiosity is so satiated with the deliverance of the Minister of Railways that they wil' not be on the qui vive. for further trade. My belief is that they will, and, as the immortal Burns puts it, if they get any in. formation, they will "prent it," and the country will know exactly what this great concern is doing.
If we are to have information, why not let us get it through the proper channel? I submit that the Department of Railways is the legitimate, proper and constitutional source from which to get information about every dollar of money expended in connection with the railways in this country. Neither I, nor the members supporting the Government, nor any other member of this House, should be charged with the responsibility of chasing around after witnesses outside of this House in order to get information. We are maintaining a department of railways with a large staff. If that staff is not adequate in order to supply this House with such information as is absolutely necessary, I am willing to accord them whatever assistance they require to obtain that information so that we may have it in the constitutional way, from the mouth of the responsible minister at the head of the department.
The floor of Parliament is the place to inquire for and obtain information concerning every department, for the benefit of the people. That is the position we take, and I think it can be supported before any intelligent audience, either in this House or outside. I am very much surprised that any earnest, intelligent member of this House should think of voting against the amendment. We have in this country nineteen or twenty different departments, every one of them a spending body. The right hon. gentleman said there was no legitimate comparison in the matter of expenditures between the Department of Railways and Department of Public Works. But, Mr. Speaker, is it not entirely a question of degree? One spends more money than the other, undoubtedly, but they both

spend money. If one spends ten millions and the other three hundred millions, are we not just as much entitled to information in the latter case as in the former? If the people of the country are entitled to know what moneys are expended in the Public Works Department, are they not, logically, equally entitled to be informed as to the expenditures in connection with the Department of Railways? I urge these arguments upon all sane men in this House representing the people. We have the following departments: Public Works, Militia and Defence, Marine and Fisheries and Naval Affairs, Interior, Agriculture, Immigration and Colonization, Finance, Mines, Justice, Labour, Post Office, Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, Customs, Trade and Commerce, the Department of the Secretary of State, the Department of the Solicitor General, the Department of External Affairs, and the Railway Department. There we have seventeen departments apart from the railways. Now, this amendment says that we are entitled to get an accounting of every dollar spent in every department in connection with the Government. Suppose we leave out the Railway Department, we say, in effect, if this amendment is not adopted, that in connection with seventeen departments, spending millions of money, we are not entitled to any information; and I gather from the attitude of the right hon. gentleman and those supporting the Prime Minister, that they contend, and will so vote, that we should have no accounting at all from any of these departments. When the members supporting the Government go back to their constituencies they will be questioned about the expenditures in the different public departments, and they will be asked "Did you vote that the House should have the information asked for?" They will have to reply truthfully "No, we voted against the amendment of the leader of the Opposition," and the people then will realize that they are not to have any information at all as to these matters.

I would like to know
whether or not my hon. friend is arguing for a reduction in the workingmen's pay?

I do not think my hon. friend could have been in the House when the amendment was read, or he would fully understand that it has nothing whatever to do with the increase or reduction of the workingmen's pay. When my hon. friend reads the amendment itself he will find that my version of it is absolutely correct. Now, Sir, I pointed out that we
have this large amount of money to spend in nineteen or twenty departments, and we have hon. gentlemen sitting in this House, and we have a Government who tell us that we are not to have any information whatever about that expenditure except what the Government, in their graciousness and good nature, may possibly bring down. We are to be something like the woman who said that she would be perfectly satisfied by feeding on the crumbs that fell from the table of her lord. We are therefore to recognize the right hon. gentleman who has just addressed the House, and his confreres in the Government, as lords of that type. We must sit down at their feet and wait for some little crumb of information to be thrown to us which they may regard as worthy of our acceptance. That is the attitude taken by the Government, and that is the position in which we are placed.
I am astonished and surprised at the stand taken by my good friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) who has come to us in this country, from the very feet of Gamaliel and who is telling us occasionally, and almost all the time, that he imbibed his Liberalism from the great Gladstone himself. Now if there is anything that Gladstone taught more strongly than another it was the principle of the people ruling and governing, of the people being placed in full possession of every item of information that was necessary for the proper carrying on of the business of the country. I am surprised, therefore, that my hon. friend should lay himself open to the chage of sinning against the light; that he should come here evidently prepared to cast in his lot with the scribes and pharisees on the other side of the House who are willing to shut out every particle of information from Parliament. I think we have demonstrated beyond all question, Sir, that we are entitled to proper information about the moneys that have already been spent, and the moneys that are to be spent in the current year. What becomes of the argument that secrecy must prevail about the business of this Government? We are satisfied to get the information that is to be found in the Auditor General's Report with respect to every department, and we should not expect to go any further. That report deals with business that has been done and finished with nearly a year ago. Is this secrecy to last forever? If railway ties or locomotives have been bought and paid for, if millions have been spent on betterments for the

national railways, and the transactions are finished and closed, surely the information with respect to them can be brought down to Parliament? Could anything be more absurd than to say that the policy of secrecy and exclusiveness is to last forever, and that after a transaction is closed and everything with respect to it is done, we in this House cannot find out how it was carried out and what has become of our money? Surely, as I have already said, what is true about accounts that we find in the Auditor General's Report should also be true, and the same practice followed in connection with the Department of Railways.
I lay down the principle, and I am not laying down aything new, when I say in regard to every department of Government that we cannot in this House depart from the principle of ministerial responsibility to the extent of one inch. We cannot do it; there is no safe ground outside a firm maintenance of that principle. The moment you abandon the principle of the responsibility of ministers in connection with the expenditure of public money you have no safe ground upon which to stand, and the people are deprived of responsible government in this country. The moment you switch the responsibility for all kinds of expenditures to any corporation, or any body of men, who are not called upon to come before Parliament and, through the proper channels, explain the situation in which they stand and the way in which they have expended public money, that is the situation with which you are faced. The Government is not simply coming to us to-day to make good the amount of $70,000,000, although that itself is a very large amount. Somebody, during the debate, spoke about it as being more than the entire expenditure of the Dominion of Canada some twelve or thirteen years ago. When the right hon. gentleman, who a short time ago was Prime Minister of Canada, issued his manifesto in 1911 he told the people that the expenditure of eighty-seven millions of money was in itself evidence of recklessness and corruption-that it evidenced that money had been mis-spent in this country. We are close to that amount to-day in the deficit in one department of Government, and yet we are told that we must shut our mouths and have nothing to say about it. What would my right hon. friend say if things were reversed, and he was standing on this side of the House and supporting the present amendment? There would then be no dic-

tionaries thrown around; the missiles would be hard rocks and they would be hurled at us in such a way that the life of nobody in our ranks would be safe. But now the right hon. gentleman is suave and calm and finds fault with any man who writes his name in black letters on white paper because it might look like "a dark lantern," or something which reflected on the character of the saintly gentlemen who sit on the treasury benches. Not only are we asked to make good this sum of $70,000,000, but any person who looks at pages 34, 35 and 36 of the Estimates will find that in connection with railways alone we are called upon to vote in the vicinity of $165,000,000, which money will have to come out of the hard earned wages of the poor people of this country. Yet we are to sit here and accept the general statement of, the Minister of Railways, which gives us no information at all upon which a right conclusion could be reached. Finally, let me say that we are asking for nothing but what is fair and reasonable when we demand that Parliament and the people be given the fullest possible information about expenditures in every department, including the Department of Railways.
Will my hon. friend allow me just one question? Who are the members of the dark-lantern brigade?
Order.

I was paired with
the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion). Had I voted I would have voted for the amendment.

I was paired
with the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee). Had I voted I would have voted against the amendment.
