Before the minister explains this item I wish to ask the Government if it is their intention, if this item passes, to go into Supply on any other department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am not aware of any reason why the question should be specially answered. The Government intends to go on with Supply according to the announcement of last night-such Supply as we can reach within a reasonable time.
Then my hon. friend intends to proceed with the Estimates of another department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I want to get an answer to my question because I understand it has been customary in this House, at least since I have been here, for one item to be taken at a time-I mean, one department -unless with the consent of the Opposition. If my hon. friend wishes to follow out the contention he made the other day that he has the right to go into Supply in any department, he may mention one day, all the departments and then the next day go into all departments, taking one item at a time, thus preventing the Opposition from proposing any resolution on the motion to go into Supply. It is not fair; if the attitude taken by the Government

on the first items of Supply is to be followed out and it is their intention to take up two or three items in one night on one motion to go into Supply, the only protection the Opposition has is to prevent the Government from passing the first item% of Supply until they tell us how many items, or how many departments they wish to go into at the one sitting.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think I see the point the hon. member has in mind. He has not expressed himself, though, correctly; he says "items" when he means "departments." Certainly we intend to pass such items as the committee feel they can fairly consider. As to the departments, I see the point the hon. member has in mind; it is that if we take up more than one department to-night we are permitted on Thursdays and Fridays to enter those departments without the consent which the rules call for. That he wishes to avoid, and I can see that there is some fairness in the contention. I would think a fair interpretation would be this: if hon. gentlemen opposite will advise us that they desire to move a general resolution against any department, I 'think it would only be fair on our side that we should not go into that department except on a day specially appointed so that the resolution could be moved. On the other hand I do not think it is right that the Government . should deny itself the privilege of going into more than one department on the same day; otherwise, I do not see how we are going to get on with the Estimates; the House will be delayed too long. The rules of the House permit it. If on Tuesday-for quite a time-the only day available for that purpose-we take only one department at a sitting we shall be going into only one department per week, and if we do that the session will be insufferably long. We have no desire in the world to avoid a motion in amendment on going into Supply if the Opposition wish to challenge any department in that way, and if they will name the particular department they wish to challenge we shall see that a motion to go into Supply, directed chiefly to that department, is made. That seems to me to be fair.

I may point out to my right hon. friend that we may wish to discuss other matters than simply those relating to one department. There are a good many subjects we would like to discuss on going into Supply. My right hon. friend knows that he can cut us off in the matter of discussion by passing from
	.
one department to another in the same night. What we are trying to reserve to ourselves is the right of discussion, not to be cut off in discussion as we have been cut off this afternoon, for example, in the matter ot information. My right hon. friend was hardly fair to the member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) when he intimated that the hon. gentleman had not expressed himself in a way that could be appreciated. I put the question specifically to my right hon. friend as to departments and he answered that he intended to go into other departments if possible. Why does he say to my hon. friend who has just spoken that he has not presented the matter intelligently?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Because he mentioned
items instead of departments and items do not mean departments.

I mentioned
departinents.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I know my hon. friend
did, and I expressed the intention of the Government. But I do not intend to exercise that intention against the right of the Opposition to challenge a department. I think that is as fair as any government can possibly be. I do not know that the Government is bound to be giving opportunities all the time, aside from the rules of the House, to the Opposition to talk about anything at all. But I do think it is fair on the part of the Government to afford opportunities to the Opposition to challenge any department, notwithstanding that we have full power under the rules to pass from one department to another. I can see that we could abuse that power, but I do not intend to do so. But surely we are fair in saying that if the Opposition will only name the department or departments that they purpose moving resolutions against, we are ready to give them an opportunity to do so by going into Supply on the department concerned. I do not think any government has ever gone that far; I am pretty sure no government will ever go further.

Why should
we be confined to the departments?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is the purpose
of the saving clause in the rules providing that we may not go into Supply on Thursday or Friday save on some department that we have been on before-so that in relation to that department a motion can be made: We do not intend to violate either the letter or the spirit of the rule.

We might
wish to discuss the civil service, for example, which is not a department. Why should we not have that right?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It can be done; there
is nothing to prevent it.

I suggest that this whole
discussion is out of order. It is purely hypothetical.

The discussion is not out of order. I raised the point the other night when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) wanted to call the estimates for his department. What we wanted to avoid was being debarred from making a motion against that particular department simply because it had been called on that particular night. Just about the time-1 raised the point the Prime Minister left the chamber and I suggested to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) that there be some understanding in the matter. During the twenty years that I have been here it has always been the rule that just before the House rose, the Prime Minister or the minister leading the House would tell the Opposition what particular business and the Estimates of what particular department would be taken up the next day. On the night before, the Prime Minister had said:	" Any department which the
Government might see fit to take up " or something to that effect. I have not the exact words, but it was repeated the next day, and I called it vague. I thought it was an answer that we did not deserve; that it was an answer that lacked courtesy. I stated at that time that, as a matter of courtesy, it had always been the rule of this House that the Opposition be informed of the work to be taken up the next day, and that the answer of the Prime Minister left the door open by him to taking up, during the discussion of Supply in Committee as to-night, items of the Estimates of more than one department thus debarring the Opposition from making a motion on Thursdays and Fridays.
I again ask for a ruling that this discussion is out of order. No question is now before the Committee.
Order.

I ask for your ruling,
Mr. Chairman. We are night after night discussing the same question, and under this item a discussion of this question is out of order.
May I correct a statement I made?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) has risen to a point of order. If the hon. gentleman desires to say anything on the point of order, I would be glad to hear him.

I will speak to the point
of order. For several nights, this House has been entertained with a discussion on this question, which is purely hypothetical. If the Prime Minister makes a motion to go into Supply required by another department the question might properly arise; but that question is not before us now at all, and a discussion of that question is altogether irrelevant to the matter which is before us and which is an item of supply. As regards the matter of discussing what is to come before us, I have sat in this House for a long time, and I have listened to the right hon. gentleman who led the House previously and also to the present hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) discussing this very question. I notice that when the answer was given to the question, the leader of the Government of the day did not confine himself to one department; that many times as many as four departments were mentioned, and then followed the statement " any other matters that might come before the House." Apart from that altogether, I claim that a discussion of this kind is purely hypothetical, and that there is before the committee nothing that we can discuss this question on.

I want to correct what
I said just now. I said that we could not make a motion on Thursdays and Fridays. What I meant to say was that we could not discuss the point.

The hon. member is
not discussing the point of order.

My hon. friend has
talked about past governments. All that I am saying now is in regard to what has happened within the past week.
We have heard enough.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would ask the hon.
member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) to remain within the rule and to speak to the point of order.
According to your ruling, if this item passes, any minister may call an item of another department, and then on Thursdays and Fridays, we will go into their estimates automatically.

That is not the point of
order.

That is the point of
order. There is nothing else before the Chair. I submit the point of order is not well taken.
We have heard a military man explaining the law; I will try, as a lawyer, to discuss the point of order as I understand it. I understand, when the Government moves to go into Supply, the rule is-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The point of order
now before the Chair is whether or not hon. gentlemen have a right to discuss the point of order to which the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) is about to refer.

I was just going to explain that I have a right to discuss the point of order just mentioned, and I wish to discuss it. The point of order is whether we can be precluded by the Government from moving an amendment to the motion to go into Supply if items in connection with more than one department are discussed at one sitting. If this is not the point of order, I think it about time that the Chairman should explain to the committee what the point of order really is.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, if I may be permitted, I should like to discuss the point of order. The question submitted to us seems to be this: Have we the right, before discussing the first item that has been submitted to this committee, to know beforehand from the Government whether or not they intend to proceed with the Estimates of any other department.
I am very glad, indeed, to have been able to find out what is the real question put before you. I think we have that right, in order to avoid such a misunderstanding as we had last week. It is important for the Opposition that this question be settled once for all. It is true that we are entitled, I believe, even after discussing a few Estimates of the various departments, to introduce resolutions on the motion for the House to go into Supply, barring Thursdays and Fridays, but we could not move concerning a particular department after the Estimates of that department had been previously considered.
Mr. Chairman, will the hon. member allow me a question?
Certainly.

What is the point of order?
[Mr. Currie. [

The point of order is to know-as I have stated previously- whether, before taking up the Estimates, we have the right to secure from the Government a statement to the elfect that they will not consider to-night the Estimates of any other department. I believe that the point of order raised by the hon. member from Simcoe (Mr. Currie) is not well taken and that we are entitled to proceed with that discussion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) has risen to a point of order which has been fully discussed by the hon. members for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) and for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). The point of order raised by the hon. member for North Simcoe is whether or not any hon. member has the right to question the leader of the Govern-' ment concerning his intentions in regard to the passing of Estimates and the number of departments which are to be taken up at the present sitting. The question now before the Committee is item No. 21 which provides for the salaries and contingencies of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Strictly speaking, the point taken by the hon. member for North Simcoe is well taken, as the question asked is not relevant to that item. The Chairman would, however, hesitate to rule that a question concerning the conduct of the business of the Committee could not be asked at any time with a view to securing a better understanding between the two or three parties in the House, and thus expediting the business of Parliament. The question asked while it was not relevant, was a very reasonable one and the answer having been given, I will now ask hon. members to return to a discussion of the item under consideration.
I notice an increase of about $9,000 in the item for salaries.

The amount
asked for is $371,612.50 for salaries, and $22,000 for contingencies. The total number of employees provided for 1921-22, as will be seen by the details, is 278, for which the total annual salaries amount to $371,612.50. The original Estimates for 1920-21 provided for 221 employees at $291,089.50. To that there has been added by the transfer of 57 employes under P.C. 2958, $49,763. That Order in Council provided that permanent temporaries employed in the different departments who came in before a certain date, and whose services were efficient and satisfactory,
\

, MARCH 22, 1921	.	1219
should be put upon the permanent list by the Civil Service Commission. Instead of these transfers being carried by outside votes, they have been transferred to civil government. That accounts for $49,763. Then the reclassification raised the salaries to the amount of $20,862.50. Adding these together we get the Estimate for the coming year of $371,612.50. For 1921-22 the staff remains at 278 employees, exactly the same as it was before. The net amount required for salary increases is $9,897. So we have in the whole service exactly the same number of employees, the increases being due to transfers and reclassification.
What are the duties of the Director of Commercial Intelligence?

The present
Director of Commercial Intelligence is one of the oldest and most experienced of our trade commisioners. He commenced service in South Africa, was afterwards in South America, and afterwards went to the war where he served two or three years. Then he was sent on a mission of inspection of trade commissionerships throughout the world. He has now taken the position of Director of Commercial Intelligence Service. He has under him the whole staff of trade commissioners. He has also the direction of the whole staff of Commercial Intelligence, which includes instructions to our commissioners in different parts of the world, the reception of reports therefrom, their examination, their editing, their publication in the Weekly Bulletin, and all the correspondence with business men in Canada who have more or less trade in connection with these different countries in which our trade commissioners exercise their functions. He is, in fact, the head of that very large and important branch.
Where is he now?

In the office
here in Ottawa. He has returned from his visit of inspection. He was promoted to his present office after competition.
How many trade commissioners are there altogether?
I could answer that more fully on a more appropriate item, but I might say we have between twenty and thirty trade commissioners.
Has the Director of Commercial Intelligence the duty of organizing trade agencies abroad? Does he advise the minister on the organization of such agencies?
Absolutely so.
Has he recommended any trade mission or agency in the United States?
No.
Has he studied that question?

Perhaps I
might give my hon. friend a short statement which would bring that matter up in a better way. We have not as a policy instituted trade commissionerships in the United States. We have none there now; we never have had.
Why?

Before the war, I commenced to study with my officers the question of the advisability of extending the service to the United States and considerable progress was made in the examination of the whole question. The war, however, intervened and it was not carried through. After the armistice I took up the question again, and since then the matter has been pretty thoroughly examined. We have not as yet adopted the policy of extending our trade commissionerships, to the United States, but the matter is now under consideration, and I hope we shall arrive at a decision in respect to it before the close of this session, because if it is decided to extend them to the United States we shall have to have legislation providing therefor.

I would suggest that
they be called "truck-and-trade" commissioners.

My own view from the first has been that there was not the same necessity for a system of trade commissioners in the United States as in more distant countries. The United States lying alongside of Canada for a distance of 3,000 or 4,000 miles, having the most intimate relations both as regards our resources and the demand and supply of both countries, with the best facilities for quick travel to and fro, with an intimate knowledge of markets and market possibilities, with the numerous interminglings commercial and otherwise between the United States and Canada, the knowledge that existed was so much greater and so much more widely distributed with reference to the United States than to other countries that there was not the same necessity for trade commissioners. Besides,

we have taken up this matter of trade commissioners in a gradual way, and the expenses in connection therewith are, of course, proportionate to the distribution. If we undertook to put commercial agents in the United States, it would be very difficult to avoid placing a large number of them there. The United States covers a wide territory, and our commercial activities extend from one coast to the other, and from the forty-ninth degree down to the southern limit of the country. All these considerations have contributed to delay and have been the reasons why the department, under former governments as under the Government of the present day, has not thought fit to extend the system to the United States.
I do not wish to be-

Perhaps the
hon. gentleman will allow me to interrupt him. I might say to him that if we agree to bring up these matters when we come to the votes for them, I think we should he able to expedite the business of the committee.
I beg to remind my right hon. friend that I am strictly within the purview of the vote.

I am not raising any question as to my hon. friend's right to put questions, and I will answer him. I am, however, just suggesting that we proceed from item to item in an orderly way. I have an item of two or three hundred thousand dollars for trade commis-sionerships and trade extension, and in connection with that, I think we can discuss to better advantage the matter which my hon. friend is now dealing with. I just put that to my hon. friend.

I put a question to the minister a moment ago: Has the Director of Commercial Intelligence the duty of recommending to the minister the organization of trade commissions abroad? The right hon. gentleman said; yes. Then I put another question: Has the minister received any suggestion from'that official as to the establishment of trade commissions in the United States? The minister replied in the negative. He said: No, he has made no such suggestion, but I have myself, with the assistance of my expert on that question, studied the matter, and thus far, owing to the war and other prevailing conditions, we have not deemed it advisable to establish such trade commissions in

the United States. Now, I say that the item which is now before the committee is a proper one in connection with which to discuss the policy of establishing trade commissions in the United States, because according to the answer given by the minister, it is within the scope of the duties of the Director of Commercial Intelligence to suggest such organizations and appointments. I must offer to the minister a humble suggestion, not in the way of drastic or destructive criticism, but for the purpose of assisting him. He is of opinion that the time is not opportune to establish trade commissions in the United States; but that time may arrive before this session is very much older, and then it will mean a vote of a large amount of money to provide for such commissions.
May I ask the hon. member what he means by "trade commission"? I fail to grasp his meaning, although I have been waiting patiently to gather the significance 6f his remarks.
A trade commission is an institution, and the trade commissioner is the officer who discharges the duties appertaining to that commission.
Hear, hear.
Listen and learn something.

My hon. friend no doubt
receives the weekly bulletins issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce, and he should know what a trade commission is, and what are the duties of a trade commissioner. By the way, may I congratulate the Department of Trade and Commerce on the publication of these weekly bulletins, which are extremely interesting and which should be of value to the trade and commerce of Canada generally. Unfortunately, in my opinion at any rate, they are circumscribed in their application, because we have no trade commissioners in some parts of the world where we should have them. The minister says that up to the present time there has been no necessity for them in the United States. On the contrary, I contend that we should have had them there for some time past. Our proximity to the United States is absolutely immaterial to the question which we are now studying. The purpose of establishing trade commissions, and appointing trade commissioners in the United States, is to open new markets in that country for Canadian industries. The situation is not

affected by any question of space, for the same distance separates us from each other. Yet the American Republic have consuls in Canada, being represented in almost every town. What are these commissioners doing in Canada?-because these American consuls accomplish here what our trade commissioners do abroad. They collect information as to the openings that exist in Canada for their manufactures, and they send that information to their State Department and keep their industries posted on opportunities that offer in Canada. The right hon. gentleman says we need not have any trade commissions in the United States because of our proximity thereto.

Perhaps it
might be of some importance to say that I did not say that.
That is what I understood.

Then my hon. friend went further than my words would warrant. What I did say was that up to the present time none had been appointed. I did say also that under all administrations no appointments had been made, that I had taken the matter up before the war, hpd suspended it, and then took it up again after the armistice, and that it was now being very carefully looked into. I gave my own opinion as I viewed the matter in the light of the past. I then said that the government was considering the subject, and that their policy would be announced before the close of the session.

The right hon. gentleman
said that but he also said a minute ago that we were so close to the Republic to the south.

I did and I said so because it was an argument why, to my mind-and it seems to have been an argument which commended itself to the department-as matters stood it was less necessary for us to have tra,de commissioners there than in other countries.
On the contrary to my mind it was much more imperative that we should have trade commissioners there.
That is all right; my hon. friend has a perfect right to his opinion.

And it is a right which I am now exercising with due respect to the right hon. gentleman. To my mind it is more imperative to establish trade commissioners in the United States because we
trade more with that country. The American Republic did not hesitate, nothwith-standing the close proximity of the United States to Canada, to appoint American consuls here. What was the net result? The net result was that they have developed an export trade to Canada of nearly $900,000,000 a year. Our lack of organization has, to a great degree, prevented the expansion of our export trade to the United States. Such an organization would have been a great assistance in the development of Canadian trade with the United States. These trade agents, established in numerous centres of the American Republic, would have opened the eyes of the Trade and Commerce Department of the Dominion to the business openings which offered to Canadian manufacturers, and in turn that department could have kept our manufacturers posted with respect to those opportunities. Then we probably could have developed an export trade with the United States which would have offset, to a certain degree at least, the 'present adverse trade balance which is so injurious to the credit of Canada. I think, Sir, that the time has come, in fact it is long overdue, when we should pay closer attention to our relations with the United States with a view to developing our export trade to that country. That opinion must have been entertained by the present Government when they brought down legislation creating the position of Canadian Ambassador at Washington. When they did that they contended that the time had come when a Canadian representative should reside in Washington and look after Canadian interests. I do not share the opinion of the Government as to the method they then suggested. I think that our representative in Washington should by no means be linked up with the British Embassy. He should not be the vice-ambassador of the British Empire in Washington, he should be absolutely untrammeled and should represent Canadian interests exclusively: If we pay for a Canadian representative at Washington, or for Canadian trade agents in that country, it is only fair that they should work for Canada first. If we send a representative to Washington who will be attached to the British Embassy the results of his work will be compiled and will be available for the benefit of those in whose interest the British Embassy is established. We know that England does not send financial agents, or trade commissioners, or consuls, or consular agents, to the United States to produce a wider market for Can-

adian manufacturers. They are live wires, they look out for British manufacturers and they act wisely in so doing. If Canada wishes to develop her trade with the United States her duty is not to reply upon other representatives, whether they bd British consuls, vice-consuls, or consular agents. Canada should see to it that Canadians who have only Canadian interests at heart are appointed. They should work for Canada. They should not report to the British Ambassador, but report directly to our Minister of Trade and Commerce for the benefit of Canadian industries. Who could blame the British Embassy at Washington for collecting and sending to British manufacturing the information that the trade agents of England collect in the United States? Nobody could blame them; they are appointed for that very purpose and they are paid out of the British Exchequer. If we want to develop our export trade to the United States we should imitate England's example. We should not put our Canadian representative Under the guidance and control of the British Ambassador, but place him under the exclusive control of the Canadian Government. To my mind this is one of the steps which this Government should take and I humbly offer the suggestion to my right hon. friend, adding that in my opinion it was imperative to have done that long ago but more imperative than ever to-day.

I am very much interested in the remarks which have fallen from the hon. gentleman, and I would like to ask him a question before we pass from this topic. He is indulging in what he himself calls constructive criticism. Following that line I would ask him in what particular line of manufactures we could increase our export to the United States to a greater extent than we are now doing?
In all kinds of manufactures.
My hon. friend is merely speaking in general terms.

Let my hon. friend wait
a minute. We have in Canada a number of manufacturers, but what is the prevailing condition? Canada is a narrow strip of four thousand miles in length and only sparsely populated. We have in Quebec city, for example, a manufacturer of boots and shoes. What must he do to market his goods? He has to travel three thousand miles to find a mere handful of customers in Vancouver or Victoria. The closer he is to the consumer the better. Now across the international boundary

line, only fifty or one hundred miles away from his factory, there is a population of millions who could use the boots and shoes which he manufactures. There is a great market at his very door, but he has not trade commissioners to assist him in obtaining it. He has not developed that market, and yet boots and shoes enter the United States duty free. If instead of catering for a handful of customers in Victoria and the other cities of British Columbia he tried to organize his market to the south of the boundary line, although he would have to meet competition there, yet he would have equal chances with his American rivals, because he can produce just as cheaply as they can.

May I ask my hon.
friend a question? Why could not that manufacturer send a traveller fifty or one hundred miles south, as my hon. friend suggests, just as easily as he could send him 3,000 miles west without a trade commissioner shepherding that traveller?
We are now discussing trade commissioners, and if the argument of my hon. friend is sound it would apply to our trade commissioners all over the world.
Not necessarily.

We have trade commissioners in England, Holland, Denmark, France and other European countries. Why should not the Canadian manufacturers send their agents over there-as so many do-and dispense with our trade commissioners? That would be the argument of my hon. friend.

I did not make an
argument; I simply asked a question of my hon. friend.

Make it a suggestion, then.
That suggestion of my hon. friend applies as well to the trade commissioners that we have already established in every country as to trade commissioners in America.
Not at all.

The Department of Trade
and Commerce is established, not to supersede the activities of our manufacturers,
, but to help them out. And if it has been found a happy medium to develop our trade in other countries, why should it not be an equally happy medium to develop our trade in the United States, where we do such a great volume of business? That is the reason why I say that trade commissioners established in the United States would be able to give valuable assistance

to our manufacturers in developing export business there.

I have no desire to delay the item, and I regret very much that the suggestion of the right hon. gentleman (Sir George Foster) was not accepted in order that we might have a more thorough discussion of trade commissioners at a future date. Evidently the hon. gentleman who has just sat down is of the opinion that the business men and manufacturers of Canada are not wide awake to the American market.
That is quite true.
He is entirely mistaken.
You are correct.

If there is anything going on in the United States in the way of business, or if there is any market opening for any of the products of the factories of Canada, our manufacturers are quite ready to do business. In fact my hon. friend will find that the very item he has referred to- shoes-is exported to the United States by our manufacturers. The functions of the commissioners operating in the United States as compared with the functions of the American consuls are entirely different. The American consul gets information, but I never yet saw one in Canada shepherding a bunch of American commercial travellers through the country. If he did so we would very much resent it.
I may tell the hon. gentleman that I have come in contact with American consuls trying to help their manufacturers to find a market in Canada.

I must have been particularly unfortunate, for I have never seen any of them. The principal thing they do, so far as my knowledge of them goes, is simply to take a fee when you make an affidavit before them and draw big salaries. They are not functioning any more than the British ambassadors are in the way of finding markets. They supply information, of course, to their government, but they are not going around looking for orders.
Now, I will say this for the Department of Trade and Commerce: In my personal experience of world trade I can safely say that no finer lot of business men could be sent to foreign countries than have been sent by the department within the last four or five years. The Canadian manufacturers owe a deep debt of gratitude to the young men who have been sent, for instance, to China, India, Japan, Australia,
New Zealand and South America. They take great pains to establish connections with our manufacturers here and to instruct us as to what line of goods we can sell there to advantage, and millions of dollars worth of Canadian goods have been sold in those markets through the instrumentality of those men. Nothing more useful has been done for Canada in fifty years than the work these men have accomplished in the last five or six years, when we needed markets badly, and when the markets of the world were open to us because German and other foreign competition was withdrawn. The fact that Canadian factories have taken the place of the factories of the Entente and supplied millions of dollars worth of goods to those countries is largely due to those clever young men sent out by the Department of Trade and Commerce. I wish to bear testimony to the very effective work they have done, and to say that this country can do nothing that is too good for them. Of course, occasionally a square peg gets into a round hole, but that has not occurred very often recently, and the work of these commissioners must commend itself to every Canadian who has had anything to do with them.
Unfortunately, for the moment our trade with Australia and New Zealand, which had reached very large proportions, is now cut off, largely due to the fact that those two Dominions have no credits with Canada. I do not wish to trespass on the rules of the House, but I would suggest that the Government should seriously take into consideration the granting of credit to Australia and New Zealand so that that trade may be continued until such time as those two countries have reached the point where normal conditions might be said to have been re-established.

What is the nature of our
shipments to those countries?
All kinds of manufactured goods.
That is general.

No, it is not general in
Australia, but I say that we have displaced Germany and England in the Australian market for most lines of manufactured goods. The depression, as the hon. gentleman has said, is general so far as those two Dominions are concerned, but that condition of affairs does not extend to China, India and Japan; their credit is ample here, and they can pay for anything ' they buy from us. Unfortunately, how-

ever, Australia and New Zealand have pot the funds now to pay for goods that they would very much like to purchase from us. They would buy millions of dollars worth of manufactured goods from us in the next five or six months if some form of credit was arranged whereby they could pay for those purchases.
In what particular lines?

Every line of manufactured goods-for instance, textiles and hardware. We have sold millions of dollars worth of hardware in Australia and New Zealand. They require all kinds of goods such as we use in the ordinary carrying on of business here, and which we manufacture. There is a good market for those goods in Australia and New Zealand, but we cannot fill that market at the present time.
I	might say also in the same connection that the Government must seriously take into consideration the question of export freight rates. If we are going to do business in those countries we must have lower freight charges. There is no use for our trade commissioners to go to those countries and get thousands of dollars' worth of business while our freight rates compare so unfavourably with the freight rates, for instance, from Philadelphia and from Pittsburg. The rate from Pittsburg to Hong Kong is now about $27, and the Canadian rate will run to $37. You cannot do business under those conditions. The last hoist given to Canadian freight rates has cut away all our foreign trade; the decline in Canada's foreign trade during the last three months is entirely due to that fact. It was freight rates that gave Germany the benefit of the markets of the world. A manufacturer in Munich would get a through freight rate to Smyrna just as a manufacturer in Hamburg could, and that rate was at least two-thirds less than from Liverpool or from London. If we are to maintain our foreign trade we must nurse it along. But I must bear testimony to the young men who have been employed by . this department as trade agents. From all quarters of the globe-Argentine, Brazil, South Africa-they send communications stating that so-and-so wants to sell certain lines of goods; that Canadian goods are known in that district and that an interchange of business is desired. Reverting to the United States, the question has been discussed of establishing Canadian 
chambers of commerce. It would be of vast benefit to this country if Canadian chambers of commerce could be established in all the large centres of the world. The offices set up in this connection would be a centre for all the Canadians carrying on business in a particular locality, a place in which our agents might have a desk when they went there, and where they could consult with the trade commissioner. I am satisfied that the foreign trade of Canada would be enormously increased if such chambers of commerce were established. As to the necessity for our having trade commissioners in the United States, I may point out that the Canadian manufacturers are wide awake to everything that is going on there, and, as the member for Red Deer would say, it would be sending coals to Newcastle to assume that we could carry on a greater trade than we are now carrying on with the United States in manufactured goods. Practically every line of business in Canada, with the exception of pulpwood and grain, is largely carried on in the United States and for that business there is a large foreign market as well as a large home market. If you go into their home market with your carloads of goods, reports will very quickly be sent to Washington of what you have been doing, and obstacles will be thrown in the way of your export trade.

Would the hon. member recommend that we renew our trade with Russia and send our trade commissioners to that country?
M. CURRIE: I was not discussing Russia for the moment. I was emphasizing the point that the establishment of chambers of commerce in such large centres as New York, Boston, Chicago, San Francisco and other places of that kind would result in our buyers going to these points and also in an increase of our sales. Now, with reference to an extension of our trade with Russia-
May I prevail upon my hon. friends on both sides to leave these big questions until we come to the big votes and to get through some of these smaller things first?

I agree with the minister, but as these matters are sometimes brought up without some of us being able to discuss them, I am endeavouring to entertain my hon. friends opposite with a

few remarks on the subject so that when the matter comes up again they will have a greater knowledge of it and will he able to discuss it intelligently.

We have done a reasonable day's work and perhaps at this late hour we might make some progress and adjourn. I am sure that the minister would prefer being comfortably at home to sitting here discussing these items.
I am ready to sacrifice myself on the altar of my country for a few hours.

So far as the member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) advances the idea that we should have trade agents in overseas countries, I am with him. I think that trade agents in overseas countries and a much better display than we have now of Canadian products in the cities of the British Isles might be of great advantage to Canada. But so far as establishing a number of paid agents in the United States is concerned, it seems to me that having regard to the present financial position of our country there is much to be done before we undertake a work of such questionable value. Now, I am satisfied that the shoe manufacturers of the city of Quebec have their travellers on the road out as far as British Columbia, a point much more distant than the larger markets of the United States. If they are able to send travellers out to British Columbia to look for business I am sure that these manufacturers or any other manufacturers in Canada would rather trust to their own trained help than to a government agent of doubtful business capacity. The business men of this country are just as able to go out and look for business in the United States as they are to go out and look for it in British Columbia and the western provinces, and I am satisfied that they can do it with greater advantage to themselves and to Canada than a government official can. For these reasons I am not prepared to follow the member for Lotbiniere in his argument in favour of trade agents in the United States. I do think, however, that any money spent in the display of Canadian goods in overseas countries will produce profitable returns and I shall be willing to support the minister in any appropriation that he may require for that purpose.

The hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) has stated that Canada has an export trade in shoes. Would he state what particular brand of shoes
are being exported to the United States, what their trade-mark is, and where they are manufactured?
I have no idea what their trade-mark is. All I know is that the United States trade returns two or three years ago showed quite an import trade in shoes from Canada.
The Slater shoe was exported for a while, that is all.

I see in the details concerning this appropriation certain items with respect to motion pictures and officials connected with that branch of the department. The right hon. gentleman went to Paris last year and I think he was there the year before as well. During his stay in the capital city of France, he probably acquired very artistic tastes. I notice, for instance, that amongst the officials of the department is an artist who is receiving a rather good salary. Who is this artist, how are his or her services hired, and what are exactly his or her duties in the department.
Would the minister, at the same time, kindly give an explanation regarding the Director of Commercial Exhibits?

It will be
quite within the knowledge of members of Parliament that for the last three or four years, the Department of Trade and Commerce has been availing itself of films as a means of educating and informing the people of other countries of the resources of Canada, what we produce, the processes of production, and certain scenic qualities of the country as well, all going to make up a propaganda of film production and exhibition. This has enlarged from year to year, and it has proved one of the most profitable investments that we have made; as being one of the most appealing methods of distributing information amongst large bodies of people. In that work, we have developed a staff which is of excellent ability and which turns out work which, I think, is not surpassed by any company or aggregation that works along those lines. You must have, in the taking of those negatives, an artist who is able to pose the situation, so to speak, so as to get your results, if it is a scenic effect, from the best possible angles, so as to produce the most catching and attractive form of what you are producing. That explains what the artist is for. He is not a painter of pictures, nor



anything of that kind. How we obtain him is through the Civil Service Commission by advertising the nature of the work and then selecting from those who apply the one who appears to be best fitted for that work. We had, as our chief director, Mr. Norrish, for two or three years. We lost him about a year ago, or a little less, because he was taken from us by the Canadian Pacific for exactly the same kind of work, but at a much larger salary than we were able to give him. _ There is, therefore, a staff which is employed in taking those negatives, in developing them afterwards and in distributing them. As to the distribution, I am sorry I have to take this on an item of an officer rather than when we come to the main vote for this work. Perhaps the information which I have given now will do for this particular thing, because when we come to that item, I should like to deal with it a little more at length, so that the House may know what we are doing along that line.
We were told by the Chairman that the details of the appropriation which is now before the committee are given at page 105 of the Estimates, and this is taken from page 105.

If I understand the matter aright, the minister is willing to give all the details in connection with officials whose names appear on page 105, but there is another item as regards distribution, and the right hon. gentleman would rather give the explanation when that item comes up.
What is that item?
The large item from which we pay the expenditures for this work.

I would suggest to the minister that when he comes to deal with the question of films and the distribution of them, if it were possible for him to give uis a moving picture of the 24,000 census enumerators, that would make a very interesting show for the House and the country.
It would cost a very large sum of money to do that, and I doubt if the object gained would be worth the expense in trying to satisfy my hon. friend's curiosity.
It would be a fine collection of Tories, and maybe the last one.
It would I hope be a collection of very intelligent men and women.
It would be an excellent exhibition of the "No patronage system" as carried on by the Government. I would like to have some information regarding the item: "Chief, foreign tariffs division, $2,610."

One part of the work of that branch-and that comes again later, although this is the salary for the chief officer-is to keep track of all the tariffs of all countries in the world. We must know in the department at Ottawa, in order to answer questions which are constantly put to us, the tariffs which rule in all the countries in the world with which we do business, and that is practically with all countries of the world. A tariff is passed at a certain time; but according to the different countries, you have modifications of that tariff by regulation, and you have to keep track of all of those. You have frequent legislative changes in the tariff, and you have to keep track of all of those. If my hon. friend wants to know the tariff upon any article in any of the principal countries in the world-and I think I may say in any of them-that information is at his disposal in the department; we are constantly being asked for that information, and we are constantly distributing it. It would be a sorry department if we did not have that part of it up to date.
That is a very important work to perform, but is all that work performed for the sum of $2,610?

That is the
salary of the chief, and you will find some others' of the staff along through the list. One man does not quite do all the work. It is a piece of work that one man could not perform by himself.

I notice that on page
105 there is the position of Director of Commercial Exhibits. This would lead one to believe that we have commercial exhibits, and a director of that service. What are the duties of this officer?

He is in
charge of two different things. We have an exhibit of commercial articles gathered from a great many countries in the world with which we do business. Our trade commissioners in these different countries get samples of the goods which are largely

in vogue in those countries. These are brought to the attention of our commercial men in Canada. A selection is made by our trade commissioners; they do not send us samples of everything that is used in these different countries, but discriminate and try to send samples of goods Canadian manufacturers might very well supply. We have an exhibit of these things in our Commercial Museum on Bank street. That is one part of the Director's duties. Then our trade commissioners have partial exhibits that they use in their offices. The Director of Exhibits has all this under his charge, their collection, their distribution, and all the information with reference to that.
Does that include Canadian manufactured products?

No, articles
manufactured in other countries, but which our Canadian manufacturers might very well be able to supply. If they visit this place on Bank street .they will see exactly the types and forms of these articles in common use in these different countries, which it would be worth while for them to undertake to supply. If my hon. friend has been a reader of the Bulletin he will see that our trade commissioners when sending in their reports, if the article itself cannot be sent, send a diagram of the article. That appears in the Bulletin, and manufacturers can see exactly what is wanted and tell whether it is worth while for them to try and supply that particular article. That has proved very useful indeed, and much of the increase in our foreign trade has been due to that kind of representation, and the representation of the article itself.

Do the manufacturers themselves take an interest in these exhibits and co-operate with the department in [DOT]making them a success I notice by the British newspapers, for instances, that the manufacturers have no less than four large exhibitions running in Great Britain at the present time for .the purpose of showing the British people that British manufacturers can beat any others in the world, and that is therefore ho use for the people to buy^ their goods outside. The British manufacturers are willing to compare their goods with those of any other manfacturers in the world. I should like to know the attitude of the Canadian manufacturer in this matter. Does he assist in making these exhibits a success? Does
78i
he co-operate at his own expense to some extent?

The Canadian manufacturer is doing exactly what the British manufacturer is doing. He is trying by exhibit of his goods, sometimes by car exhibit, sometimes by local exhibitions, and in every other way possible to show to the people of Canada that he can manufacture the goods they need just as good as anybody outside. We do not help him in that; he does the whole of it at his own expense. If my hon. friend has ever had the good fortune to go to the Canadian National Exhibition, as it is called, in the city of Toronto, which is held in the last week of August and the first week of September, he will have seen there a most wonderful exhibit of the products of our manufacturers, to speak of only them for the time being. They have the latest and most up-to-date equipment there, and their own representatives on the spot, able to give out information, distribute literature and so forth. Although that is the largest exhibition, there are others in a smaller way throughout all of Canada. That is the business of the manufacturers; we do not help them in that. What we help them in is in getting them samples of goods that are largely used in other countries, and which we think the Canadian manufacturer might very well make. When they see these samples they can make up their minds whether they will fill the bill in those countries in respect to that particular form of manufacture. To that work we bend our energies, and ask the Canadian manufacturers to take advantage of the exhibits we make for that purpose.

It might be interesting for the committee to know "that on Thursday last a gentleman by the name of Mr. Halladay, a brother of the hon. member for Bow River, addressed a small gathering in the Railway Committee room. This gentleman had travelled around the world representing a Canadian company, the Canada Cycle and Motor company, and his address was, I think, one of the most interesting and illuminating I have ever listened to. During the course of the year he had travelled over 41,000 miles. He had started out from his headquarters in Canada, crossed the Pacific to Japan, travelled extensively through Japan and China, gone down to the islands of the Pacific, Sumatra and Java, then to Australia and New Zealand, India, South Africa, and back home again. One interesting fact he brought out was that during the war Japan had built

up an enormous foreign credit balance. The result of that was that the merchants of Japan were buying largely outside of their own country. That had an adverse effect on the manufacturers of Japan, so the government of that country stopped foreign credits in an endeavour to compel the citizens of Japan to purchase from their own manufacturers. Their attitude in that respect was very much like the attitude of those in this country who try to prevent the Canadian people from buying merchandise outside their own country, even though they can buy to better advantage. The hon. member for North Sim-coe (Mr. Currie) spoke of some obstacles in the way of Canadian manufacturers obtaining trade outside of this country. In my judgment, you cannot hope to make a success of foreign business in this or any other country unless you buy from the country where you sell. You cannot expect to sell to any great extent unless you buy from that place. That means, in my judgment, that the tariff in this country which prevents importations will also limit exportations to foreign countries. I am sorry there was not a larger number of members present to listen to the very excellent and instructive address of Mr. Halla-day. His remarks were certainly interesting and illuminating. A point he made clear was that all the goods sold by his concern outside of this country were sold at a profit. It is held that goods sold by Canadian manufacturers outside Canada are sold at cost of production or at a loss sometimes to keep factories going. His claim was that the goods sold by his concern in foreign markets were sold at a * profit and that their goods were sold to the consumers in Canada at higher prices than abroad.
I want some information on item 4, at page 105, regarding the expert in grain chemistry. Who is this expert at the present time?

This has reference to the grain laboratory in Winnipeg. Dr. Birchard is director. My hon. friend knows that we have been carrying on through that laboratory certain experiments, for instance, in regard to the conditions of wheat, as respects moisture, and how they affect the keeping of wheat in transport and storage. A very important part of the work of that branch has been the experiments in connection with milling and baking, which have been carried on now for two or three years. And we are publishing each month bulletins which give the results

of the milling and baking te,sts. Experiments are made in regard to different kinds of wheat and how they pan out in these processes. Dr. Birchard is director, and has a staff of three who, with him, carry on that laboratory.
Monsieur le President-

Does this official report
directly to the department or to the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada?

He works in
connection with the Board of Grain Commissioners and also report to the department. He is estimated for in the civil government, and is, as my hon. friend will see, an officer in the department, being under its instructions. But there must be in all these matters of experiments, etc., strict collaboration between himself, the Board of Grain Commissioners and the inspector in Winnipeg.
Monsieur le President-
Does he submit his reports to the Board of Grain Commissioners first, and after they are dealt with by the Board, are those reports passed on to the department?
My impression is that he reports to the department direct, and sends a copy of the same report to the Board of Grain Commissioners. I know we keep records here.
Monsieur le President-

There is a considerable doubt in the minds of some people 'as to how that works. We are looking for good things from that laboratory in Winnipeg, but so far as we are concerned, there seems to be little information available, and what there is to be obtained is difficult to get at. Some people are under the impression that he reports to the Board of Grain Commissioners, who censor those reports and then pass them to the department. That is the point upon which we desire to be clear.

That is not so; we do not get censored reports, but the original documents. I would call the attention of my hon. friend to this fact, which he will realize the moment I mention it. With regard to tests of grain as to moisture conditions* and their influence on either transport or storage, and so far as the quality of grain is concerned for milling or testing purposes, it is im-

possible to set a laboratory to work and expect results within the first year or two. The best results cannot be obtained for several years, because of the differing conditions from year to year. You must get a series of experiments over a wide area and extending over a reasonable period in order to strike the average result. During the first years of experimentation there was very little distribution of information. Now that period has passed and the director has got upon more solid ground. There is a wider basis for deductions and recommendations, and these brochures or bulletins are being now issued regularly with an authority which they could not have in the more experimental stage. If my hon. friend has not experienced any good results from the work that has been carried on, I can assure him that we have numerous and very strong commendation! of what has been done.
Monsieur le President-

I do not want to be understood as saying that we have received no benefit from this work, for such is not the case. We are, however, of the opinion that we are not receiving the benefits which we should expect. One of the principal things which we anticipated would be the determination of a reasonable spread between different grades of grain, but we have not seen any action in that direction so far. The spread between different grades is as wide this year as ever, if not wider.

My hon. friend will admit that there is a wide difference between the application of what may be considered as knowledge, absolute or concrete, of the qualities of different grades of grain, and the devising of means by which that knowledge will be put into practice in the actual process of buying, because the process of buying depends upon so many other considerations than the quality of wheat, that the spread is sometimes very large, often much larger than it ought to be. It is very difficult to find out how to apply scientific knowledge to buying in the market towns.
Monsieur le President-
I should like the minister-
Are you through?
I desire to finish the point I am discussing.
Monsieur le President-
Mon honorable ami (M. Maharg) a la parole.
Mais qu'il acheve.

If I understood the minister correctly, he said that this chemist determined the amount of moisture that grain should carry in storage, or words to that effect. Has the present chemist anything to do with determining the amount of moisture that grain should contain in order to enter a certain grade, say, No. 1 Northern grain? Does he determine the amount of moisture it should carry?

I do not think that element is considered in the grading of grain. Whether it is possible to do so or not I do not know, but practically it has never been done up to the present time. It may be that in time we may add to the tests for the grading of grain, which are now largely mechanical, some scientific principles, which have been ascertained by results in the manner suggested; but up to the present time the mechanical methods, of touch and sight have been those used for determining the different grades.
Carried.
I quite appreciate the anxiety of hon. gentlemen to get away at this hour of the night, but this is one of the matters that we in the West are largely interested in.

I rise to a point of order. The hon. member for Maple Creek voted earlier in the evening against the Government giving information, and therefore I cannot see why he should insist upon obtaining information now.

If I desired to enter into any discussion of the point that my hon. friend has raised I could give him a very apposite reply. The point that we would like to be clear on is-who does determine the amount of moisture that grain shall carry to permit of it entering into the different grades?

I am not an expert in the business, but in so far as I have seen it carried one, the grading is done by the inspectors or the graders after having taken a sample from the car. The grain is placed on the table of the examiners and they grade it according to its plumpness, or otherwise, and its color. That is done either by the eye or by touch.

As to making a moisture test of each grade I judge that is not done. However, I am not an authority on the subject and I would have to ask my officers for information in respect to it.
We are within a few minutes of midnight. Does not my right hon. friend think we have been discussing these matters long enough?

It is true that we have been discussing them at some length but we have not made any progress. I cannot conceive of such an intelligent body of men as I see before me spending all this time upon an item and leaving without adopting it.
If we pass this item will it satisfy my right hon. friend?
I am entirely in the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite. Of course the progress of the business depends very largely upon them and if they do not want to hurry matters I am in their hands.

In the closing days of last session the right hon. gentleman himself, in almost the last words uttered by him at that time, criticized us because we passed a lot of his Estimates without studying them sufficiently. He made reference particularly to the Estimates of the Department of Justice saying: "You discussed a few legal questions, but when you came to the Estimates themselves you rushed them through, and you did not even discuss a few which to my mind were objectionable or at least questionable." Well, Sir, tonight we have studied to the best of our ability the Estimates which have been submitted to us. The details of the item which is now under consideration cover more than a page, and I think it is only reasonable that we should now adjourn so that we can give to the item the attention which it demands. My hon. friend from Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) is seeking a lot of information from the minister and I shall do my best to assist him in getting it. I support very heartily the suggestion that we adjourn.

The hon.
gentleman has supported the item for the last hour and a half, and I am sure we will never have any lack of questions so long as he is in the same state of mind that he is to-night.
I have a lot of questions to put when the minister's estimates are again taken up.

(Translation.) It
seems to me that if I appeal to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the language in which he is now a master, he will accept my suggestion. It seems to me that we have done a good day's work. The minister himself, during half an hour, endeavoured to arrive at a definition of what is and what is not confidential. He has wasted half an hour of the hon. member's time on this subject. The Deputy-Speaker has settled most difficult questions of order in a very satisfactory way foi himself and perhaps for the House. I do not think it necessary that I insist on the matter. We were interested witnesses of the minister's acrobatic feats, and pyro-technical dialectics, and I think we may request this from him because he is a wise man, a man of experience, a man who attends to the country's business; he must be in favour of the eight-hour day; if he is not, he deserves that all good labourers in this country vote against him at the next elections, and there will be enough electors voting against him in the next election contest to oblige him to give the labourers some encouragement. I am not here to make a speech; it is midnight, time for us to disappear, let us finish.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I have listened with dose attention to my hon. friend's suggestion. He has discussed-yes, he has discussed, and discussed, yet, I do not think he has shown any good reason for an adjournment. There is no necessity, because it is twelve o'clock, that the committee adjourn without having passed a single item. After such a varied and eloquent debate, we should pass a few items and then we could enjoy a good sleep on a peaceful conscience.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Before the item carries I
would like the Minister of Trade and Commerce to repeat in English his French speech of a few minutes ago. I did not understand one word he said, and I think it is his duty in regard to these items to give the information which he imparted in French to us all.
It is not necessary that every member on that side of the House should understand French.

The Estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce are perhaps one of the most important set of

Estimates that this House has to consider, and it seems to me that at this early hour of the morning-it is one minute past twelve-the minister should not ask us to pass an item of over $390,000 for salaries, especially in view of the fact that so very few Government members are present. It is quite evident that those gentlemen are carrying out the wish they expressed tonight when they voted for no information. There is a great deal of information which we would like to have, and although I might, of course, move that the Chairman do now leave the Chair, which motion would carry because we have more members present on this side than are now in their seats on the Government benches, I do not wish to take that course, and I respectfully ask the minister to report progress.
I have no desire to press these Estimates unduly, but I think we should pass this item. If any information is required I shall be very glad to give it.

As my right hon.
friend has proved his love for the French language, I would ask him to publish his weekly bulletin in French. That is a most desirable and necessary improvement.

I will take it
into the most sympathetic consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Before the item carries or the committee adjourns, I would like to tell the minister that the Canada Year Book published by his department is most incomplete in regard to the educational institutions in the province of Quebec. Some of our most important colleges are not even mentioned as educational institutions, although many of them have been active for over a century.

I am very glad my hon. friend has called attention to those omissions, and when we come to the item provided for the Canada Year Book I shall have the information for him. These educational statistics have only been attempted within the last two or three years, and if any lack of information is noticed it is certainly a kindly act on the part of any member to call attention to it.

There is an item here for the Dominion Statistician. I asked the right hon. minister yesterday for information about the census enumerators in the county of Pontiac, because previously I had written to the Chief Commissioner and he
told me that the appointments had not been made. I understand that the Government endeavoured to make appointments, but as some Ontario men were appointed I have no doubt the ministers representing the province of Quebec objected. The minister told me that the appointments had been made, but I have not been able to ascertain the names of the commissioners. Would the minister be good enough to give me those names now?
I have not the names at hand now. When I answered my hon. friend yesterday I told him that the appointments had been made; that is correct.

That is, permanent
appointments?

Yes. The chief trouble was in reference to the geographical situation in the county of Pontiac. In the end we divided it into three parts of one division. Temiskaming is the most populous part and as it would be necessary for one of the proposed appointees to travel two or three hundred miles to take up the work there, I have made arrangements whereby a resident of Temiskaming shall act for that part of Pontiac.

Would the item under
consideration include the Dominion Bureau of Statistics?
That would include the Civil Government employees, but not the work of the statistical department; that is a separate vote.

Does that include the
salaries of the remaining employees of the Board of Commerce?
No.

Is there a special item
for those salaries?
Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No. Mr. Chairman. There are several items here that we would like to have some information on. What is " Chief Transportation Division?"

The Statistical Department has a very wide field of work, and amongst other things it has to prepare statistics of the different transportation systems, which was formerly looked after by the department of Railways and Canals. The Statistical Branch of that department has now been merged

with the General Statistical Department, and this is the officer who attends to that branch of work.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, at page 105 of the Estimates there is an item as to a "lecturer," which can be translated by the word "conferen-cier." Could the hon. minister say whether or not that lecturer gives lectures in both languages and whether or not he is qualified to give them in French and in English?

In the first
year and part of the second year during which we were commencing and perfecting the preparation of films we put on a series of exhibits of these films and visited about sixteen or eighteen of the principal cities of the Dominion, commencing at Halifax and passing through Westmount. The pictures were explained by a lecturer and they formed, I am sure, a valuable contribution to the information of the people generally as to what we are doing in the department. They were received with apparent satisfaction, the tributes offered in that connection being very numerous.
I find on pace 105 the following item: "1 chief, division of demography, $3,960." What class of work is demography?
It is really the taking of the census. The word comes from the Greek "demos," the people, and " graphn, " a writing.
Is the Dominion Statistician, who is at the same time Census Commissioner, also chief of the division of demography?
No. The chief of the division of demography works under Mr. Coats.
What is his name?
E. S. Macphail. He is one of our older civil servants in that department, and a most efficient man.

As I understand it, the Dominion Statistician collects facts with reference to men and women and things, whereas the chief of the division of demography would collect only facts with reference to human beings. Am I right in that?
I do not quite see the distinction between men and women and human beings.
The minister misunderstood me. I said men and women and things-inanimate things.

Oh, I think the Dominion Statistician does more than that. He is director of all the varied activities of the Statistical Department, which are not confined to simply counting men and women and inanimate things and tabulating them. He has under him a very large staff.
Mr. Macphail is actually in charge of the taking of the census?
Yes.
Then where does Mr. Coats fit in?

Just as the
director of a large business establishment fits in over numerous branches and divisions of the business controlled by him.

In the Auditor General's Report Mr. Coats' salary is given as $4,000, while on page 105 of the Estimates it is given as $4,800 for 1920-21, and $5,100 for 1921-22. Will the minister explain the difference?

Probably it is
due to reclassification.
The same thing applies to the demographist.

And the same reason would apply.
